To further enhance the evaluation of these algorithms, the framework provides a set of metrics for assessing their accuracy. The framework's capabilities are demonstrated through a comprehensive benchmarking test of several prominent semantic mapping algorithms, which are evaluated within a diverse set of 1,000 simulated scenes.

Rikudo is a Japanese board game with strategic elements and a unique combination of elements from both Sudoku and Dominos. Research has been conducted to determine the complexity of Rikudo. By transforming Rikudo into Generalized Remi, a more comprehensive version of the game, multiple approaches were explored. However, these attempts ultimately failed to yield a polynomial time solution. Yet, by drawing inspiration from Sudoku, a more limited version of the game, was discovered to be polynomial time solvable. A more in-depth examination of Rikudo, utilizing a reduction method, revealed that Rikudo is in NP. Furthermore, it was demonstrated that Rikudo is also computationally hard, and therefore, its solution cannot be efficiently found. Rikudo is a unique game, with a high level of complexity, making it a valuable subject for further study.

Optimal transport theory, a geometric probability tool, has expanded its scope to address machine learning challenges, notably in the large-scale analysis of data pairs. This research focuses on solving large-scale Optimal Transport problems, where the sample size and/or matrix dimension exceed a million. To achieve this, three computational methods are explored. Firstly, a technique combining fast Fourier transforms is introduced for calculating pair-wise OT costs and evaluating the OT distance. Secondly, a Bregman OT algorithm is developed, utilizing a specific generalized entropy, to efficiently compute solutions. Thirdly, a gradient descent approach is implemented using a powerful graphics processing unit to solve large-scale OT problems represented in sparse matrices. Our methods are evaluated on benchmark datasets from diverse fields including medical research, text analysis, image processing, and more. Our results confirm that these techniques can efficiently solve large-scale OT problems, with running times as low as 1 second, yielding 100 times faster outcomes compared to existing methods.

Ramanujan, in his 1921 paper, proposed a set of conjectured integral identities that connected modular forms and cubic forms in integers. He initially shared these with G.H. Hardy, later publishing them in his second paper on integral identities. In this research, we prove several of Ramanujan's integral identities using a specific mathematical approach that connects congruence properties of integral forms and Hecke groups. We also discuss an alternative method for proving these through the application of Maass forms and Hecke operators.

We have conducted a detailed analysis of eight multiple-image quasar systems, utilizing the ESI instrument on the Keck 10-m telescope. Our study, which involves spectroscopic observations of quasar systems with strong lensing, dark matter, and caustics, has resulted in new redshift measurements for seven lens galaxies. These measurements, along with photometric redshifts for the eighth system, have been used to assess the accuracy of strong lensing models. Our analysis has also led to the discovery of velocity variations in quasar photometrically active systems, specifically in HE 0433+2041, SDSS J1004+1100, and SDSS J1205+0159. These observations will contribute to our understanding of the distribution of mass in cosmic scales and enable the testing of theories that explain the behavior of gravity.

In this work, the analytical and numerical solutions of the nonlinear q-fractional diffusion equation are investigated using the fractional modification of the Lie symmetry method. The resulting q-fractional equation is used to derive a consistent system of equations, allowing for the determination of the Lie point symmetries. These symmetries are used to obtain a new set of q-fractional recursion operators, which in turn lead to the development of the one-parameter exponential contraction mappings. An extension of the fractional recursion operators is also introduced, allowing for the derivation of the explicit solutions. The study is further complemented by the development of the q-fractional characteristic equation and the construction of the invariant functional. A numerical example is provided to illustrate the effectiveness of the method, highlighting its ability to obtain solutions that are consistent with the physical principles of the theory of the fractional calculus.

The phonon Hall effect has been observed in various insulating solids with broken time-reversal and inversion symmetries. Recent experiments aim to uncover the mechanisms driving this effect, with a particular focus on the role of a previously proposed vector current. Our work delves into the topological nature of the phonon Hall effect, examining a specific model that exhibits a particular type of symmetry breaking. By analyzing this model, we reveal that a non-trivial topological property, tied to the phonon's Berry curvature, underlies the effect, validating the predictions from the model. Our analysis also uncovers a link between the topological charge and the phonon Hall effect Hall coefficient, offering valuable insights into the topological nature of the phenomenon.

A significant challenge in Raman imaging is achieving high signal-to-noise ratios in large fields of view.  One of the most effective approaches is shifted excitation Raman spectroscopy (SERS), which utilizes distinct excitation wavelengths to collect Raman spectra at each location in a sample.  However, this method is limited by the need to scan the sample with multiple excitation wavelengths, making it difficult to achieve the desired signal-to-noise ratios.  To overcome this issue, we have developed a novel method that employs the Nod and Shuffle UV-Vis camera technique to perform SERS imaging on a 1.2x1.2mm field of view.  This method, which utilizes a UV-Vis camera to collect two different excitation wavelengths, allows for the acquisition of Raman spectra at a single wavelength and the elimination of the need for scanning the sample with multiple excitation wavelengths.  This method, which was tested on a variety of biological samples, has demonstrated excellent signal-to-noise ratios and the ability to acquire detailed Raman spectra.  Additionally, the method has the potential to be used for a wide range of applications, including biological, environmental, and industrial fields.

Investigation into Fejér and Størker inequalities for matrices led to derived inequalities such as Fejér and Størker inequalities for matrix operators and their inverses. Building on these, Levin and Størker inequalities were formulated for matrix functions. Matrix versions of well-known inequalities such as the Størker-Hölder inequality and the P\'{o}za inequality were also obtained. In addition, relationships between these operator-to-operator inequalities were established, including a generalization of the Levin-Størker inequality.

We investigate the mean null energy condition for both Schwarzschild and Friedmann-Robertson-Walker black holes that undergo evaporation. We find that in the case of Schwarzschild, the condition holds as the evaporation process proceeds. Notably, this result holds in the near extremal regime, a finding that contradicts a previous study. Additionally, we discover that in the near extremal regime, the total null energy density approaches zero asymptotically. In the context of Friedmann-Robertson-Walker, we find that in the near extremal regime, the condition holds as time progresses. A novel consequence of our findings is that the extremal black hole can be seen as a null fluid with zero null energy density in the near extremal regime, suggesting a more accurate representation of the evaporation process.

In conformal field theories, we apply the methods of conformal perturbation theory to compute the dimensions of various operators, including the Heisenberg operator, the scalar operator, and the partially conserved multiplet operator, in both even and odd space-time dimensions. We confirm that our findings align with existing literature when dimensions are predicted to be identical, and highlight the implications of our novel results for cases where dimensions are previously unknown. Our calculation of dimensions for partially conserved multiplets offers a new approach to computing the viscosity of the stress-energy tensor in various space-time dimensions, and the Chiral Anomaly in the $SU(N)$ QCD anomaly. Our results also have potential applications in computing the viscosity of the stress-energy tensor in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

Recent attacks on critical infrastructure have highlighted the vulnerability of
modern society to Information Warfare and Cyber threats. Although the
vulnerability of industrial systems is a long-standing issue, it has become a
major concern due to the growing risk of being exploited by nations for
strategic gain. This paper introduces a new cybersecurity testing framework
specific to ICS, known as the ICS Cybersecurity Testing Maturity Model (ICS-
CTM2), which is designed to assess an organization's total security
management processes. By outlining the process for evaluating the effectiveness
of an organization's cybersecurity measures, ICS-CTM2 provides a practical
methodology for assessing security management within Industrial Cybersecurity. This
paper outlines the development of ICS-CTM2, its core components, and the
benefits of implementing it for assessing an organization's cybersecurity
capabilities.

In complex environments with limited resources, multiple agents must adapt their strategies to optimize their collective effectiveness. As these environments evolve over time, the agents must quickly adjust their actions to achieve the best results. A new approach called GBW represents an agent's value in changing scenarios, using the products of past rewards and reducing unnecessary computations to improve performance in dynamic settings. By testing this method against established algorithms in challenging scenarios, such as coordinating to reach a goal in limited time, the results show GBW performs as well as or better than established competitors, even when the conditions become increasingly difficult.

A particular form of social prejudice called stereotypical bias affects many areas of language processing. Current methods for evaluating this bias are limited to a single stereotype at a time, making it difficult to get a complete understanding of the social bias present in language models. Our research introduces a new approach that looks at how different stereotypes are interconnected, allowing for a more comprehensive assessment of prejudice in languages. We also propose a new dataset called StereoSet, consisting of 120,000 labeled sentences, to make this kind of analysis possible. Using StereoSet, we examined three cutting-edge language models to discover the prejudice present in them and found that these models harbor numerous prejudiced biases that are closely linked. We hope that our research and resources will facilitate further study on this topic and contribute to the development of more equitable and unbiased technologies.

To optimize distribution grid electrical tilt, we introduce a new off-policy learning method that ensures real-time optimization efficiency. Leveraging a deep neural network as a model of local policy, our approach optimizes an actor-critic electrical tilt policy based on a sample-based cost function that accounts for power loss, voltage deviation, and dynamic grid constraints such as branch current limits. The electrical tilt policy is trained using off-policy samples from historical controller data, enabling us to analyze the effectiveness of our proposed method in a numerical setting compared to an optimal policy approach. The results show that an actor-critic policy learns to mitigate voltage deviations and branch current limits while minimizing power loss, with the learned policy exhibiting good generalization to new scenarios and adapting to changing conditions in real-time.

A combined assessment has been performed on data from multiple LHCb searches regarding the CKM angle $\gamma$. Direct measurements from these searches are consistently accurate to a precision of around $2.5^{\circ}$, while a unified analysis incorporating additional information from a variety of B decays yields a more precise measurement of $\gamma$, estimated at $(71.1^{+1.3}_{-2.2})^{\circ}$. The main source of error in the assessment is associated with specific CP observables from B$_s$ decays involving b quarks.

The article delves into the intricate aspects of ellipsoids with higher-order symmetry properties in two or more dimensions, focusing on those with minimal dimensions exceeding two, and explores their structures, characteristics, and foundational frameworks. It also examines, in detail, the properties of two-dimensional ellipsoids exhibiting cross 2-fold and quadruple symmetry, and the properties of four-dimensional ellipsoids exhibiting octuple symmetry.

To better understand the risks and opportunities presented by personal data markets, we conducted a study with 40 participants from the financial sector, examining how they respond to potential transactions. Our findings reveal that individuals are cautious when deciding whether to sell their data, prioritizing privacy above all else. The data we collected is currently being analyzed for publication.

We propose an advanced deep learning method to efficiently identify the received symbols when using quicker-than-Nyquet (FTN) signaling in systems that transmit information. By training a deep learning model on patterns resulting from FTN transmissions, we develop a faster and more accurate algorithm called FTN list sphere decoder (FTN-LSD). This algorithm combines a deep learning-based search engine with a reduced complexity model to detect the received symbols. Compared to the traditional maximum likelihood decoder, our method significantly reduces computational complexity while maintaining low computational overhead. We also show that the proposed system can achieve a higher data rate than traditional QAM systems while maintaining the same complexity. Numerical results confirm that the proposed FTN-LSD outperforms existing soft-decision decoding algorithms, such as the minimum BER algorithm, by as much as 90%.

This paper focuses on essential features of the order topology for effect algebras and their connections to (1) Frink ideals, (2) the Riesz decomposition property, (3) the projection generated effect algebra, and (4) the solvability of the effect algebra's positive and negative parts in the effect algebra's unitary norm.

Recent research has demonstrated that saliency techniques can be effectively utilized for data augmentation, thereby enhancing model performance.  A novel approach, SaliencyMix, has been developed to improve model performance by utilizing saliency techniques in conjunction with Mixup.  SaliencyMix aims to improve Mixup by generating mixed samples that are tailored to individual samples' specific saliency patterns.  A unique method has been designed to calculate the weighted combination of mixed samples that are centered around each sample's unique saliency map.  Additionally, SaliencyMix incorporates a novel loss function that is centered around each sample's saliency map.  To ensure that SaliencyMix does not lead to overfitting, a dynamic threshold is dynamically adjusted based on the saliency of generated mixed samples.  A series of experiments were conducted on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K datasets to evaluate the efficacy of SaliencyMix, with the results showing that SaliencyMix outperforms Mixup and other state-of-the-art data augmentation strategies.

Let $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}(G)$ be the infinite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke algebra for a finite group $G$. Specifically, it encompasses the group algebra of $G$ when considering a field of characteristic zero. Previous research by Arakawa and Frenkel introduced a class of "good" elements within the Iwahori--Hecke algebra, and it was found that these elements give rise to well-defined traces on $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}(G)$. Our contribution offers a proof that every trace on $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}(G)$ is inherently associated with "good" elements.

We're proposing a new and more accurate method of testing gravitational theories using galaxy alignment measurements, which involves analyzing how the orientation of bright galaxies within a study area changes over different scales. This method can be applied to small areas, and its effectiveness doesn't rely on comparing local and large-scale data. We'll test this technique using a modified gravitational theory called Horndeski gravity, which includes theories like bimetric and scalar-tensor gravity as specific cases. Our analysis will involve simulated data of galaxy orientation measurements within a large area, and we'll assume that the orientation of each galaxy's central part can be measured accurately. Our results show that our new method can distinguish between altered Horndeski gravity and general relativity, even when the orientation of bright galaxies within a small area is measured accurately.

In non-Newtonian fluid mechanics, the unique relationship between stress and rate of strain influences the fluid's behavior over time. Our research focuses on colloidal suspensions of soft particles, specifically investigating the unorthodox rheological properties exhibited by deformed soft particles that return to their original shape. By employing particle-based simulations that accurately capture the particles' deformation kinematics, we explore the effects of varying inter-particle forces and fixed dimensionless parameters on the rheological properties. Our findings reveal significant non-Newtonian effects, including time-dependent behavior that cannot be explained by a single exponential decay. Furthermore, we observe that the particles' ability to change their deformation responses due to applied gradients, resulting in a nonlinear shear response, is a characteristic feature of the rheological properties. Additionally, we investigate the effects of particle softness and deformability on the stress tensor's symmetry, as well as the related linear response functions. Our results demonstrate that the stress tensor's anisotropy is a direct result of the non-uniform deformation responses due to applied gradients, with the anisotropy's magnitude increasing with softer particles and greater deformability.

The study of the growth and melting of nanoparticles has far-reaching implications for a wide range of technological applications across various fields. Despite its importance, the melting process of nanoparticles has not been thoroughly understood, primarily due to the difficulty in obtaining experimental measurements of the melting temperature and time dependence. In this research, a data-driven approach is employed to develop a physical model of the melting of 40- and 100-nanometer gold spherical nanoparticles, using a combination of experimental data from transmission electron microscopy and a phase-field model. The results reveal the nanoparticle's melting temperature and time dependence, which are found to be significantly lower than that of bulk gold. The study also provides a comprehensive characterization of the phase-field model, highlighting the impact of several key physical parameters on the melting kinetics of the nanoparticles. The research demonstrates a generalised framework for combining experimental and computational approaches to develop a robust physical model of the melting of nanoparticles, with potential implications for a range of materials systems.

This is the beginning of a series focusing on the concept of dynamical gradient structures for the $p$-Laplacian with Neumann boundary conditions. In this first paper, we develop a general theoretical framework for parameterized splitting theorems and bifurcations in a broad context. This framework serves as the foundation for future research, where we will move to more specific applications, such as the $p$-Laplacian with p ranging from $p=2$ to $p\in (1,\infty)$.

The concept of taste tasting is a complex, subjective phenomenon influenced by numerous factors such as food characteristics, cultural and social norms, individual expectations, and even physiological responses. As a result, the interpretation of taste varies significantly across different cultures, impacting how people perceive and enjoy various foods. This research aims to create a three-dimensional model that maps taste data from distinct cultural backgrounds, including Western, East Asian, and African traditions, using data from surveys and discussions. By tracking the evolution of this model over time and incorporating diverse perspectives, this model can serve as a valuable tool for cultural exchange, facilitate a deeper understanding of taste variations, and foster a more inclusive appreciation of food.
We derive a set of novel identities for (h; q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials. The proof of these identities is accomplished using the fermionic $p$-adic q-Vicki umbral operator.

In numerous medical trials, the long-term effects of treatments remain a key area of interest.  Due to the fact that patients typically stop taking medication during the course of a trial, there's a significant gap in available data when analyzing the effects of long-term treatment use.  In order to address this, researchers often employ an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, which assesses treatment outcomes based on the initial assignment of treatment. However, the ITT approach has its limitations, as certain non-compliant patients may have significantly different outcomes than those who adhere to treatment protocols. In an attempt to address this, we've developed a new approach that utilizes reinforcement learning methods to estimate long-term treatment effects while considering the effects of time-dependent treatment decisions. By modeling the entire treatment duration as a sequence of discrete time periods, we've developed a policy model that enables the estimation of optimal treatment policies. Furthermore, the model can be used to calculate treatment effects while accounting for non-compliance. The proposed method can be integrated with existing data from observational studies and RCTs, including covariates and time-dependent treatment decisions. The effectiveness of this model has been demonstrated through simulation studies and a real-world study on diabetes patients.

In research, identifying the root cause of a disease using observational studies can be complicated by factors such as recall error and exposure recall bias. People often misremember their past health and exposure habits, which can lead to biased estimates of disease and exposure associations. We propose a method to control for this bias using the counterfactual model and the concept of "memory of the past". Our method uses data from control groups to create a hypothetical memory of what would have been recorded if the individual had no disease. We then use this information to simulate how an individual's past might have been remembered if they had remained disease-free. Our semi-parametric causal model uses this information and other constraints to estimate the effects of exposure on disease, taking into account how memory might have been biased. We also present a method to estimate the bias parameter and evaluate its performance in different scenarios using a simulation study and apply it to real data from a Swedish cohort study of kidney disease.

Generative models can be used for data analysis by learning the probability distribution of data, as opposed to simply representing it. This is because the former allows for the estimation of latent variables and therefore joint densities, while also enabling the calculation of evidence lower bounds and comparison between different models. Unfortunately, this approach often results in worse fit latent dimension and often leads to worse reconstruction quality in comparison to autoencoder training. This work investigates the effect of using reversible layers in generative models, specifically how they impact the estimation of latent variables and latent dimension. It is demonstrated that exact maximum likelihood training of reversible autoencoders matches the estimation results from non-bayesian training of reversible autoencoders. This is further supported by the analysis of real-world data, where it is shown that the estimation of reversible autoencoders is less accurate than that of non-reversible autoencoders.

The concept of Smart Cities has gained prominence as cities strive to enhance residents' quality of life and facilitate informed decision-making through abundant data analysis. However, the vast amounts of available city data often hinder its effective utilization. To address this challenge, we present an innovative data analysis framework that empowers users to extract meaningful patterns from city data, facilitating the identification of potential issues and strategic investments. This framework integrates the Single Value (SV) method with the Multi-Value Pattern (MVP) approach to identify correlated data features. Users can interactively analyze city data attributes through our visualization tool, enabling the detection of associated variables. Case studies conducted on real-world Montreal and Toronto data reveal that our MVP pattern-based analysis is more effective than traditional Single Value analysis in identifying relevant correlation patterns.

This research explores the development of an efficient algebraic multigrid preconditioner for systems derived from the reaction-diffusion equation and the generalized Stokes equations using the HDG-P0 method, which combines high-order divergence-free variables with continuous pressure variables. We leverage the intrinsic inf-sup stable HDG discretization to design geometric multigrid preconditioners, which significantly improve the system's condition number and scalability. Numerical experiments reveal our proposed preconditioning strategy outperforms existing methods, especially for systems with varying diffusion coefficients, showcasing its robustness.

Missing data in studies causes problems in interpreting results, and this issue is widespread in fields like observational studies and clinical trials. While sensitivity models can be used to estimate the reliability of findings when data is missing, they require a long time and large expenses to apply them in practice. In this study, we introduce a new method to estimate the influence of missing data using Bayesian analysis, and it can provide a quantitative measure of the reliability of results when data is missing. Additionally, we propose a metric called the E-value to estimate the reliability of results when data is missing, and it can be calculated quickly in minutes, regardless of the amount of data. Our study shows that the E-value has a similar result as the sensitivity model in assessing the reliability of results when data is missing.

In crossover trials, missingness in treatment response data is a common issue, which can compromise the reliability of analysis methods based on this data. This problem is particularly acute in crossover trials where multiple treatment periods are collected from each participant. A novel statistical approach is developed to handle missing responses in crossover trials. This approach uses multiple imputation techniques to account for multivariate missingness. The analysis model incorporates a within-subjects model for each treatment period, adjusting for carryover effects in later periods, and a between-subjects model for the overall treatment effect. The proposed method is applied to a clinical crossover study of patients with asthma, using the predication procedure and Bayesian inference.

A new category, referred to as $\text{WMon}^1_{\text{Sc}}$, is introduced with a specific class $\mathcal{S}$ of monoidal categories, featuring a particular type of weak monoidal framework. This category, $\text{WMon}^1_{\text{Sc}}$, is characterized by a groupoid structure, allowing for the classification of weak monoidal frameworks up to a weak natural isomorphism. This classification is further connected to a specific type of combinatorial object, referred to as an associahedron, which is defined for any given finite sequence of integers. This associahedron serves as a key component in categorifying the Teichmüller complex, originally introduced by Losonczy and Matheus, within the context of $\text{WMon}^1_{\text{Sc}}$.

DRAM is currently the leading memory technology in modern computing systems, but existing designs lack the ability to accommodate customized functionalities and energy-efficient solutions. To address this, researchers have developed a new approach called CODIC, which is an adaptable substrate that enables the integration of diverse in-DRAM functionalities, such as custom data encoding and compression, at reduced cost and energy consumption. By utilizing CODIC, developers can implement in-memory computations using a framework that is compatible with existing DRAM technology, allowing them to create customized memory blocks with minimal additional overhead. The design of CODIC is based on a modular architecture that is composed of a set of standardized functional units, a memory management system, and a power delivery network. To ensure scalability and flexibility, CODIC incorporates multiple types of functional units, a dynamic management system, and a modular design of the memory blocks, allowing developers to choose the components that best meet their needs. The design of CODIC is exemplified by two custom memory blocks, one for log compression and one for approximate computing, that demonstrate significant energy savings and speed improvements while maintaining high data accuracy. The development and validation of these custom memory blocks demonstrate the effectiveness of CODIC in meeting diverse system needs.

This paper is the second in a series that explores the role of functional programming in designing and managing virtualized networks. It delves into network evolution and design principles by illustrating the development of both simple and comprehensive computer networks. By doing so, it demonstrates how functional programming can be leveraged to streamline the process of network evolution and thereby accelerate innovation. A distinct approach to writing programs for network design and management is proposed, which contrasts with existing methods, and this methodology is demonstrated through concrete examples. Furthermore, the paper discusses the significance of program composition in network evolution and how it can be utilized to facilitate network growth and adaptation.

To explore the feasibility of generalizing the two-qubit X and Y operations in a toric code to its multi-qubit counterpart, we first developed a method to approximate these operations using a combination of Clifford gates, the iSWAP gate, and a phase gate. The resulting approximation was found to closely match the two-qubit operations, exhibiting identical logical state properties and unitary behavior. Building upon this finding, we then generalized the approximation to multi-qubit operations, encompassing a broad spectrum of states. In the process, we discovered that the logical state properties are preserved, demonstrating the potential of this method to expand the two-qubit operations for a variety of logical states within a toric code.

A working observatory consists of multiple interconnected components, including devices, systems, and processes. To effectively manage a garden-orchard-observatory, one must integrate observational research with resource allocation, processing tasks, and data acquisition. A key challenge lies in unifying disparate tasks, each having unique requirements, within a cohesive framework. We present a new task control system called OPUS, based on standards from the VO, which enables the scheduling, monitoring, and execution of complex scientific tasks. OPUS is now operational at the OPUS-DCS observatory and can be fully integrated with the OPUS-DCS hardware at https://obs.astro.univie.ac.at/.

As modern society's reliance on wireless technology grows, there's a pressing need to educate students about complex wireless networks. However, traditional educational methods often prove ineffective in teaching large-scale systems with numerous interconnected components. To address this issue, this paper presents an innovative approach called Interactive Digital Educational Platform (IDEP). By integrating a simulation engine, basic modeling skills, and gamification elements, IDEC enables students to interactively model and optimize complex wireless networks. Through IDEC, students can design their own networks, simulate scenarios, and track the evolution of network parameters, which in turn drives engagement and learning. Real-world data from multiple courses shows that IDEC can effectively educate students about large-scale wireless networks.

The widely accepted relationship between ozone and molecular oxygen has been questioned by certain studies, which have suggested that both gases might be generated by photochemical processes that do not depend on the initial O2 abundance. In order to assess the validity of the O2-O3 correlation on exoplanets, we have reevaluated this relationship through photochemical simulations of Earth-like atmospheres containing N2, CO2, CH4, O2, and CH4, with H2O also considered as an intermediate in the O2 production pathway. The simulations revealed that the O2-O3 correlation is robust, stable, and consistent across different models, with O3 concentrations varying linearly in response to changes in O2 abundance. The results of these simulations are in agreement with observations of several terrestrial planets and moons, as well as with theoretical models of non-hydrocarbon atmospheres. The O2-O3 correlation is also expected to remain consistent on Earth even if future climate scenarios involve significant CO2 reductions, with O2 being completely depleted in the atmosphere, and CH4 being replaced by increasing concentrations of N2.

The non-equilibrium behavior of electrons in a one-dimensional system with a varying potential leads to the emergence of directed currents. These currents can persist even when the underlying potential is time-averaged and is a result of a non-equilibrium response. This phenomenon has been observed in a two-dimensional model, but its behavior on a constant strength infinite potential wall in three dimensions remains unexplored. Using numerical simulations of a three-dimensional model featuring a Hofstadter bubble lattice, we demonstrate that a similar non-equilibrium response occurs when the electron transport is confined to a specific one-dimensional path. These findings suggest that a non-equilibrium current can indeed be sustained in a three-dimensional model, even when the electron transport is concentrated on a single path with a constant potential wall in one direction.

Recent studies have shown that Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (NMT) can be a suitable replacement for the traditional phrase-based Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) approach. NMT models can directly generate translated text, offering improved readability. Our investigation focuses on enhancing multilingual NMT models for specialized medical translation tasks, using the Medline abstracts from the PubMed Central database as source texts and machine-readable MeSH thesaurus terms as targets. To refine these models, we employed a novel semi-supervised approach, training them on a parallel corpus of human-synthesized translation pairs and supplementing them with unaligned general medical corpora. Our experiments demonstrate that this training method leads to a substantial 11% decrease in the average edit distance to the human reference, resulting in a 20% drop in the average number of insertions needed to match the human reference.

A theoretical study using a two-fluid model has investigated the modification of altered-ion-acoustic waves in a plasma system consisting of hot electrons, cold ions, and a superposed dust continuum. The model takes into account positive dust grains and ion temperature. Analytical solutions for both solitary and shock waves were obtained using the re Reduced-Senft Equation, which was numerically verified by the Particle-in-Cell method. The findings indicate that the presence of dust grains and ion temperature significantly alter the wave dynamics. High dust-to-ion mass and ion temperature ratios lead to altered-ion-acoustic shock waves, while increased dust Grain-to-ion mass ratio generates altered-ion-acoustic solitary waves. Ion temperature is found to have a more significant impact on shock waves than solitary waves, and the dust Grain-to-ion mass ratio has a greater effect on shock waves than solitary waves. Nonthermal electrons were found to stabilize their own acoustic modes but have minimal effect on altered-ion-acoustic waves.

This research introduces an innovative language-independent approach to 
constructing sentence representations, focusing on cross-lingual information sharing. 
The method is based on a multi-task learning framework where sentence 
representations are derived from sentence pairs in different languages. 
A novel loss function is proposed that encourages the model to align similar 
sentences across languages and distinguish similar sentences within the same language. 
Additionally, an unsupervised technique is employed to align sentence 
representations between languages, leveraging contextual information to align 
corresponding sentences during alignment. 
The model is trained on parallel sentence datasets and then fine-tuned on 
a multi-lingual text database for compact retrieval. 
Experimental results on a multi-lingual test set demonstrate that the model 
significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, with a 10.3% improvement 
in recall at 10 and a 5.2% improvement in recall at 100.

Multimodal learning's effectiveness heavily relies on a crucial concept: selecting and prioritizing relevant modalities. Current approaches typically choose specific modalities for different tasks or inputs, but these approaches are often hindered by two main limitations. Firstly, they're restricted to using pre-determined modalities for input representation, which can be overly restrictive and neglect the potential of combining multiple modalities. Secondly, they're unable to dynamically adjust the modalities based on the task or input, which can lead to underutilization of available information. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel method called Prototypical Modal Adjustment (PMA), which learns to select relevant modalities by analyzing prototypical examples from each modality. PMA is capable of dynamically adjusting the modalities based on the task or input, as well as leveraging the unique strengths of each modality to improve overall performance. Furthermore, PMA can be seamlessly integrated with existing methods to enhance their performance. Through a series of experiments across multiple datasets, we demonstrate that PMA not only surpasses existing methods but also excels in various scenarios, including low-resource and zero-shot learning environments.

The standard theory of particle scattering in heavy ion collisions, grounded on classical transport theory, has been a successful application in studying heavy ion interactions. However, this formalism has a known limitation when it comes to describing scenarios in which the energy of the photons emitted and absorbed by nucleons is not negligible. This restriction becomes a significant issue at low energies where the energy of the photons makes up a substantial portion of the energy of the emitting nucleon, ultimately affecting the description of phenomena such as photon production and coherence effects. The development of a new classical transport theory aims to overcome this limitation, allowing for a more accurate description of particle scattering and photon interactions at low energies. This new theory, founded on the modified eikonal formalism, accurately models the scattering process by considering the initial and final conditions of both particles and photons involved in the interaction. The modified theory, presented in this research, has been rigorously tested and validated through comparisons with quantum scattering theories and experimental data. The study also provides a detailed analysis of the modified theory, its underlying principles, and its application in heavy ion collisions.

This research introduces a new method for building neural networks specifically designed to optimize spoken command recognition for autonomous vehicles. A standard approach to this task involves collecting data, labeling it and using machine learning algorithms to analyze it. Our strategy involves employing a network structure that combines a traditional neural network with a reduced-dimension approach to process acoustic data, and we have found that our approach can achieve a DCCS metric of 65.88 at a training set size of 4000 samples, which is comparable to or exceeds the performance of established models like the ResNet model. Additionally, we have also seen improved performance when using our approach in conjunction with other widely-used models such as CNN, LSTM, and attention-based networks.

The theory of quantum-jump evolution offers a straightforward approach for calculating the probability distribution of the number of jumps an open quantum system experiences over time. This is achieved through the use of Lindblad and Kossakowski-Dysudski master equation representations. This paper explores the possibility of the existence of multiple Lindblad operators capable of yielding the same quantum-jump probability distribution. This concept is demonstrated through a case study involving a three-level system and an environment consisting of two incoherent states. It is shown that the number of jumps in this context can be accurately represented by four distinct master equation expressions. This includes one using Lindblad operators and another using Kossakowski-Dysudski operators, as well as two alternative expressions using non-Hermitian and non-Lindblad operators. This finding highlights the non-uniqueness of the quantum-jump formalism.

We have conducted a computational study to investigate the effect of plasmonic aluminum nanostructures on the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells. Our investigation involved examining the influence of these aluminum nanostructures on the absorption characteristics of different thicknesses of hydrogenated amorphous silicon thin films. We discovered that the gold counterpart of these aluminum nanostructures outperforms them in terms of efficiency, but we also explored the effect of different shapes of aluminum nanostructures on the absorption in silicon thin films. Our results show that the circular and prolate spheroidal structures perform similarly in terms of total absorbed light, but the oblate spheroidal structure surpasses the other two shapes in absorbed light for thicker silicon thin films.

The properties of computational complexity can be analyzed in different programming languages that support various programming paradigms. To compare these languages, researchers have created abstract complexity classes based on various logical systems, which capture various notions of time and space complexity. This paper examines the relationship between the language PTIME and a first-order logic system, particularly its interaction with a specific operator that enables quantification, as well as its impact on the emptiness problem of regular languages. To measure the complexity of regular languages in different languages, researchers have introduced a parameter that captures the number of operations required to solve the emptiness problem. This paper explores the connection between this parameter and the notion of boundedness, which can be expressed using first-order logic systems, as well as its implications for the complexity of different languages.

In recent years, researchers have been pushing the boundaries of artificial intelligence (AI) by utilizing deep learning techniques to enhance video understanding. As AI technology advances, advanced video intelligence applications are emerging in various fields, including surveillance, security, and military operations. The rapid growth of deep learning models has led to a substantial increase in the complexity of neural networks. Consequently, the need for more efficient video processing has become increasingly pressing. To address this challenge, this paper presents a novel approach that combines algorithmic and hardware optimizations to accelerate Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for video identification, utilizing Hierarchical Tucker Tensor Decomposition. The proposed technique is characterized by three key components: a unified framework for decomposing LSTM networks using HTD, a model pruning method that reduces the computational complexity of HTD-decomposed networks, and a hardware architecture that accelerates LSTM processing based on HTD-decomposed networks. The results demonstrate that our approach can significantly reduce model size and accelerate inference times, and that the proposed hardware architecture can yield a 3.5 times speedup in processing decomposed LSTM models compared to traditional methods.

The MAVLink protocol, used by popular UAV systems like Ardupilot and PX4, has long been unsecured, leaving it vulnerable to remote tampering since its inception. Despite past security issues with canary-based detection, a comprehensive analysis of MAVLink's security is still lacking. In this research, we conduct a thorough examination of MAVSYS components and the MAVLink protocol, identifying potential security risks and vulnerabilities associated with remote attacks on UAV systems. We develop a comprehensive security framework, MAVSec, to ensure the protocol's integrity, using canary-based detection to safeguard critical messages from malicious modification. The framework, integrated with the PIX4 Flight Software, successfully protects MAVLink communication, making it the first fully secured open UAV system available to the community.

The majority of current network research operates in a controlled, non-mobile environment. However, various experimental platforms such as software-defined networking and others, require the simulation of dynamic topologies.  We introduce a distributed topology emulation tool called Kollaps, which replicates the packet flow between multiple, distributed BGP networks in real-time, using a collection of interconnected nodes.  Kollaps is designed to facilitate the study of complex network behaviors resulting from BGP interactions, routing policies, and dynamic changes in network topology.  Utilizing Kollaps, researchers can easily replicate various scenarios such as BGP route manipulation, network outages, and malicious control, across a wide range of networks, including large-scale infrastructure.  Initially designed for the BGP Mirror project, Kollaps can be applied to a wide range of applications.
The Newman-Penrose map's null points correspond to null cones in twistor space.

Researchers have developed a novel muon detector designed to create detailed maps of the Earth's underground structures using low-energy X-ray photons generated by muon decay. This innovative detector leverages the unique characteristics of plastic scintillators and ceramic components to provide exceptional light output and a low thermal connection coefficient. Prototypes of the muon telescope were constructed by combining different materials and tested in a laboratory setting, resulting in a thermal noise reduction of up to 91% when compared to conventional plastic scintillator alternatives.

This paper proposes an extension to the LL(1) parser framework by incorporating parsing expressions, enabling a more expressive and more robust parser generation system, as parsing rules can now be rewritten to improve parser generality, particularly in dealing with precedence and associativity.

This research investigates the phenomenon of vacuum Cherenkov radiation in a $U(1)$ gauge theory, specifically at high temperatures, with an emphasis on how it relates to the electroweak phase transition. The study assumes that the Standard Model's Higgs field behaves similarly to a fermion with a small mass gap, and considers the impact of both zero and non-zero temperature on the process. It also explores the potential connection to the Standard Model's phase transition by calculating the relativistic relaxation time associated with the process and comparing it to the rate of the phase transition. The analysis employs a framework based on the Bethe-Salpeter equation and the Furry picture, and involves a numerical evaluation of the associated vertex function.

To gain insight into the workings of human language comprehension, we employed cutting-edge deep neural networks on extensive linguistic data, examining the unfolding process of predicted words over time to identify the neural circuitry involved. Our findings indicate that the human brain utilizes a diverse array of processing strategies when predicting words in context, rather than relying on general rules, according to the linguistic complexity and word's inherent ambiguity. This methodological approach not only provides a foundation for future research into neural language modeling but also offers a comprehensive framework for measuring the predictive power of language models.

We propose a straightforward yet robust approach to determine the three-dimensional positioning of objects by observing as they rotate. Most object positioning techniques rely on changing viewpoints to gather diverse angles, albeit they require a 360-degree vantage point to calculate positioning. In contrast, we suggest utilizing the fact that learning from viewpoints where objects are fully visible is less complicated than from partial perspectives. Observing an object as it spins allows for a single viewpoint to gather a range of angles. We develop a method where the optimization of an object's positioning is directly linked to the rotation, allowing for a single step optimization. A novel data collection approach is also introduced where object rotations are induced through minimal actions such as tapping. We demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms other techniques in accuracy and requires fewer training samples, and we also show improved results on real-world datasets.

In quantum structures consisting of superconducting and normal regions, connected via electrical leads, the movement of Cooper pairs can be observed. When a single particle is injected into the superconducting area, the formation of bound states occurs, resulting in the emission of two particles at specific energy levels. This research demonstrates the ability to control the ratio of particle emission through superconducting or normal channels by adjusting the bias voltage of the injecting lead. Theoretical modeling, based on the Blonder-Kummel-Nevir (BKN) formula, has been applied to explain the phenomenon. The experiments reveal that the movement of Cooper pairs is accompanied by the reflection of single particles, influenced by the presence of the second superconducting lead.

To study high-energy emission from solar flares, a new model is developed to analyze particle acceleration in magnetic reconnection. This model incorporates ad hoc angle-scattering at the boundaries of the reconnection region, leading to a decoupling of the velocity and pitch angle of non-thermal particles. As a result, the particle distribution evolves more uniformly in velocity space. To compensate for the reduced acceleration of particles in the high-velocity range, additional heating at the X-point is included. The model shows that the distribution function of non-thermal particles becomes self-similar at late times, leading to a power-law index that depends on the scattering mechanism. The model also predicts the emergence of two distinct populations of accelerated particles, with one population accelerating more efficiently. The model's predictions are consistent with simulations that involve significant anisotropic scattering, and it may be applied to study the acceleration of cosmic rays in the interstellar medium.

We explore the potential for enhancing our understanding of the Standard Model's extended scalar sector by combining two high-precision measurement approaches: leptonic Z$^0$ experiments and hadronic Higgs decays to photons. This is driven by the possibility that nature of the electroweak phase transition could be classified as a first-order transition, which we assess by examining the feasibility of detecting a significant difference in the Standard Model predictions for the $\Gamma(\Gamma_{Z})$ and $\Gamma(\Gamma_{H})$ decay widths. The study reveals that such a difference could be observable at future lepton colliders, including the ILC, CEPC, and FCC-ee, but not at the LHC. Conversely, we find that Higgs decays to photons are sensitive to a second type of transition scenario, known as the "crossover" scenario, which we investigate by analyzing the impact of non-zero mass splittings within the scalar sector. The study demonstrates that Higgs decays to photons are more effective at probing these mass splittings than lepton collider experiments, with the FCC-hc offering the best possible scenario for such investigations.

The combined numerical radius of a matrix is defined as the maximum value of the norms of its singular value decomposition and the absolute value of its off-diagonal entries in a specific order. This paper proves the differentiability of this quantity with respect to some specific matrices, while also investigating its subdifferential. The authors then apply these results to the spectral value.

The concept of differential privacy has gained significant attention in recent years, and numerous studies have been conducted to assess its applications across diverse fields. However, the current literature lacks a comprehensive examination of differential privacy in the financial sector. This paper aims to investigate the potential applications of differential privacy in finance, specifically focusing on the key challenges that arise when this concept is applied to financial data. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a framework that outlines essential requirements and considers them from both a privacy and security perspective. Furthermore, this study provides a detailed analysis of the proposed framework and its implications for the financial industry.

This research paper explores the concept of stochastic mappings as a generalization of random fields, originally introduced by J. Perkov in 2001, which can be viewed as a formal representation of a transformation applied to a random set of points in a multidimensional space. Building on this idea, we develop a framework based on a correlation theory for stochastic mappings that establishes a stochastic version of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for random vectors. We leverage this theory to derive a set of relationships for random dispersion fields, which can be seen as a transformation applied to a random field, resulting in a new field. We then demonstrate that these relationships can be expressed as a generalized version of a partial differential equation, with the random field as the initial condition.

Researchers have been exploring the possibility of using high-energy lasers to initiate combustion in high-pressure, flammable hydrogen-oxygen mixtures for propellant ignition in future rocket propulsion systems. To achieve this, they conducted a series of experiments using a high-energy, nanosecond laser pulse with a power density ranging from 10 to $10^6$ W/cm$^2$ to ignite a mixture of oxygen and hydrogen at 100 mbar with a concentration of 16%. The results showed that ignition occurred at laser power densities above $10^4$ W/cm$^2$ and reached maximum temperatures of up to 4000 K. However, the team was unable to determine the optimal power density for ignition due to the low resolution of their diagnostic equipment, which limited their ability to accurately measure combustion dynamics. To address this limitation, they developed a novel technique for analyzing combustion dynamics that uses a high-speed camera to measure the evolution of flame front structures during the ignition process. The new method provides detailed measurements of flame front thickness, growth rate, and propagation velocity, which can be used to study combustion dynamics in high-pressure, high-temperature gases and optimize ignition conditions for future rocket propulsion systems.

In real-world image segmentation tasks, particularly in medical fields, accurately determining object boundaries is crucial. However, current state-of-the-art boundary-agnostic models often sacrifice boundary precision to prioritize object shape, which can be a significant drawback for applications like medical imaging, where detailed boundary analysis is essential. To overcome this limitation, we developed a novel boundary-conscious model, named the Boundary-conscientious Network (BNet). This model, which can be efficiently trained on a mobile device, utilizes a unique 2D feature extraction technique and a boundary-focused decoder to effectively capture intricate object details. To further enhance portability, our BNet model is implemented using the Tensorflow Lite library and seamlessly integrates with mobile applications. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted experiments on two datasets and achieved superior results, surpassing those of other state-of-the-art methods in both boundary accuracy and object shape precision.

This research introduces a driver messenger system, enabling communication between drivers through a novel, two-way interface. The system comprises a text input panel, similar to those found on smartphones, and a text display panel mounted on the dashboard. An experimental version of this system has been built and tested in a near-driver study to assess its usability and effectiveness in facilitating driver-initiated communication. The results demonstrate that using a driver messenger system can enhance driving performance when drivers are informed of critical events by other drivers.

The movement and distribution of non-interacting particles is being studied using computational models, specifically in an unconfined environment with no external forces acting upon them. The added effect of weak propulsion forces, similar to those generated by flagella or magnetic tethers, is considered. The interaction of these propulsion forces and the boundary of the container is being examined to see how it influences the overall behavior of the particles and their tendency to become localized at the edges of the container. The study reveals that when the propulsion forces are sufficiently strong, the particles will eventually escape localised regions and start to diffuse out into the open space.

Within the Average Particle Model, we incorporate Siegert states by using a solution that is modified from the standard Schroedinger approach. This modification involves replacing the discrete bound state eigenfunctions in the particle model with a continuum version, specifically with a finite width. Siegert states in the Average Particle Model exhibit strong coupling to the continuum, yielding a complex energy width that aligns with experimental data for the ground state of the alpha particle. Notably, this modification does not alter the particle model's ground state energy or the ground state probability density outside the nucleus.

Observations of the Si IV 1398 nm line in a solar flare were made using the Interface Wide-Field Imaging Imaging Spectrograph on the International Space Station, allowing for high-resolution tracking of spectral and spatial characteristics during the event.  High-resolution observations at a 7.7 ms cadence revealed rapid changes in the line's intensity, with the initial increase occurring within 5 seconds and extending up to 175 km along the line of sight.  A notable feature of the event was the presence of a low-temperature, nonthermal broadening component, which peaked at 1400 K, and an even warmer feature extending along the line of sight.  Analysis of the event revealed a nonthermal velocity of 3.5 Mm/s, which is consistent with the estimated magnetic field strength of 100 G and the coronal loop's length of 80 Mm.  A flare model based on these data suggests that the event began with reconnection in the low corona, releasing energy into the line of sight.  A flare model based on these data suggests that the event began with reconnection in the low corona, releasing energy into the line of sight.

The strong CP problem, tied to the strong $\theta$ vacuum, has been a longstanding enigma and has recently been revisited as a potential solution to the quantum gravity phenomenon. In the context of string theory, it's been shown that axions are guaranteed to exist, however their specific properties are complex and difficult to predict. We will outline a general framework for strong CP based on strong-weak duality, which can be applied across a broad range of string models. Furthermore, this framework allows for the axion to be the source of both the strong CP phase and the quantum gravity scale.

The impact of the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the irradiation flux on the critical angle of ordered thin films is investigated using a free energy model that considers both thermodynamic and kinetic effects. A key finding is that the FWHM has a negligible impact on the critical angle when the $Q$ value is much greater than the FWHM, allowing us to simplify the analysis by setting the $Q$ value to zero. This simplifies the analysis and reveals that the critical angle is determined solely by the interfacial energy between the ordered and disordered phases. When the $Q$ value is comparable to the FWHM, a kinetic barrier to vacancy formation and migration at the interfaces must be overcome, and we find that the required vacancy diffusion length is related to the FWHM of the irradiation flux.

To prevent unauthorized use of copyrighted software, a novel approach is introduced that utilizes C# implementation of the Pathway method. This new technique involves modifying an executable's binary files, specifically the Pathway headers, and then distributing them. The recovered header information will contain data on the regions protected in the original executable. When a potential user attempts to run a copy of the software, its executable will identify the protected regions, and upon detecting these regions in another executable, it will inform the owner that the recovered regions cannot be matched with any unprotected regions in the original executable.

We demonstrate the multiple convergence of a certain series of mean square convergent type automorphic Dirichlet series, with no assumption on the growth of the underlying weight. We also show that if the series are effectively bounded, then their partial sums will have a certain property called complete convergence. Finally, we provide several concrete examples to illustrate our theoretical findings.

This article explores the potential of forming a subgroup in a semigroup near to a specific subset of the semigroup. A semigroup S with an involution'fixes the form of elements within it, determined by the laws governing S and the definition of involution. A semigroup near to a subset A in S is a subset B in S where every element in A has a counterpart in S. We establish several results on near subgroups in semigroups featuring an involution, including semigroups in a particular class of semigroups 'S'. In these semigroups, the forms of elements are determined by monogenic subgroups. We demonstrate that a subset A in S is a set of generators for a semigroup near A if and only if A contains a full monogenic subsemigroup. A subset A in S is a semigroup if it contains the identity element and is equal to its own inverse. We prove that a semigroup near A in S is a semigroup if and only if A is a semigroup near A in S. We also find that a subset A in S is a semigroup if and only if A is a semigroup near A in S. A subset A in S is a left-right semigroup if it follows the left-right semigroup laws. We find that a left-right semigroup near A in S is a semigroup near A in S. A subset A in S is a right-left semigroup if it follows the right-left

We have developed an efficient statistical method for estimating a log-concave probability density function in d-dimensional space. Our approach combines Mixture of Factor Analyzers with maximum-likelihood estimation and local scaling techniques. In high-dimensional data sets with fewer than 100 data points, our method significantly outperforms existing mixtures and kernel density estimators in terms of integrated squared error. Our improved algorithm utilizes a novel, high-performance mixed-integer programming solver based on advanced branch and cut techniques. This novel solver can efficiently process large Mixture of Factor Analyzers with large numbers of components and dimensions. Our algorithm is highly scalable, allowing us to tackle density estimation problems in millions of dimensions using mixed-integer programming.

To efficiently sample stable granular systems with fixed volumes, we developed a novel approach based on the Wang-Landau algorithm, which generates an effective Boltzmann factor for arch-based configurations. This method is capable of handling massive systems with millions of particles and computing the associated partition function. It effectively identifies the most stable configurations within a system and provides an accurate estimation of thermodynamic quantities, including the average volume and its standard deviation. Moreover, our method reveals that the Boltzmann factor exhibits a smooth, monotonically decreasing pattern, allowing for a precise calculation of the largest free energy difference in the system.

We formulate a game model for a two-player competition between adventurers and directors on graph domains. Each graph node represents an adventurer's location, and the directors' actions are restricted to creating or removing locations and determining availability of movement. Adventurers can choose their next move from unoccupied, available graph nodes or those temporarily exempt from movement restrictions. A win is achieved when all adventurers reach a designated destination graph node. Analysis focuses on the long-term survivability and convergence to equilibrium in strategies employed by the directors, and corresponding impacts on the adventurers' movement strategies.

The fluctuation spectrum of a stochastic process provides the basis for understanding the dynamic properties of the process. Traditionally, the spectrum is calculated through ensemble averaging, but recent findings suggest this method can be replaced by averaging over numerous process realizations at a specific time frame. This alternative approach, known as a spectral density of a single realization, has been explored in detail. In this paper, the relationship between the spectral densities of Gaussian processes at different frequencies is examined, and it is shown that these relationships depend on the covariance and autocorrelation functions of the process. Furthermore, the study reveals that the statistical properties of the spectral density can be accurately described by a Gaussian distribution in the case of stationary processes.

This study delves into the interaction between two distinct soliton solutions of the (1+1)-dimensional Broer-Kaup system, classified as rational first-order autonomous nonlinear non-periodic higher-order solitons. To achieve this, the necessary condition for the invariance of the system's Lax pair under the transformation was determined. Ultimately, two types of interaction solutions were derived using the bilinear method.

This study focuses on one-dimensional incompressible Euler equations under periodic boundary conditions, where the initial density and viscosity are constant, and we consider weak solutions to the associated Cauchy problem that exhibit irregularities in the initial velocity. Our goal is to prove a global $L^2$ bound on the vorticity and the conservation of the energy of the Euler equations for such solutions, which is a result not achievable through traditional methods utilizing the energy equation directly. To overcome this limitation, we employ a technique of integrating the Euler equations in combination with the continuity equation to derive an integrated form of the Hodge-Laplace equation, and we then utilize the regularity results from our prior work to establish the existence of the bounded vorticity set associated with the incompressible Euler equations.

The Virtual Reality project, VIRUP, aims to develop a simulation of a parallel universe, allowing users to experience it as their own, employing advanced game technology and interactive simulations. Users will be able to interact with a virtual world modeled after their real life, enabling the creation of an immersive experience. Through the combination of gamification and user-defined simulations, users will gain valuable insights into their behavior and well-being. As they progress, they will unlock new interactions and decisions, shaping their virtual existence. The ultimate goal is to increase users' self-awareness and reflection in their personal lives.

In today's data-driven society, understanding basic data literacy is crucial for future generations. To address this, we developed a board game called "Space Voyage," which aims to teach young people about data (primarily targeting those aged 12 to 18) in an enjoyable manner. This game-based intervention leverages the principle of data physicalization, making abstract data concepts more tangible and engaging. Initial findings from our experiments indicate that "Space Voyage" successfully enhances users' data skills, such as evaluating datasets and visualizing data trends, and also fosters positive attitudes towards working with data.

In software-defined networking (SDN), the logical structure of a network is represented by the data-plane, which is composed of individual packets. When a new logical connection is established or an existing one is torn down, a data-plane is involved. SDN-driven networks are capable of fast and efficient setup and teardown of data-flows, thanks to standardized control protocols. The widespread adoption of SDNs has led to the creation of large-scale, high-speed data-flows in data-planes, which are characterized by massive amounts of data being generated from various sources. Consequently, these data-flows are often processed by large-scale data-streaming systems, such as the Apache Hadoop and Apache Spark. The performance of such systems heavily depends on the data-flows, including the volume of data being transferred, the speed of data arrival, and the frequency of streaming operations. This paper presents a novel approach to identifying and analyzing these data-flows in SDN-driven data-plane environments. The proposed solution is based on a novel data structure, which is capable of storing and analyzing multiple concurrently active data-flows in a single pass. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solution, which is implemented using a data-flow identification library called FluD. The library is designed to be flexible and extensible, allowing it to be seamlessly integrated into various data-parallel processing engines.

Recent years have seen a growing interest in disentangled representation learning. However, current approaches often require additional information about the structure of the data, such as how different factors are related. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework that learns a basic form of disentanglement by leveraging relationships between factors in the data, rather than assuming a specific structure. Our approach is inspired by the principle of invariance in invariant learning and achieves similar results in certain domains without needing additional information. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in both synthetic and real-world image datasets, including the MNIST and CIFAR-10.

A cutting-edge device known as the oscillating foil turbine is poised to revolutionize ocean energy harvesting from ocean currents, with its innovative technology outperforming traditional wind turbines. By utilizing the rapid changes in pressure and velocity around the oscillating foil, this turbine can generate a substantial amount of energy. This research focuses on understanding the complex interactions between the foil and its wake, particularly in the initial stages of the foil's movement. By studying the energy exchange between the foil and its wake, this research aims to develop a more efficient energy collection system using multiple foils. To achieve this, this research investigates the energy efficiency of a tandem setup of two foils, with the second foil positioned in the wake of the first one. As a result, this research reveals that the second foil experiences increased energy input from the wake, with its energy collection significantly improved. Notably, this is evident from the significant boost in the Strouhal number, with the energy input increasing by 50% and the wake velocity by 25%. This research also provides a comprehensive explanation of the complex pressure and velocity patterns in the wake, with a focus on understanding the movement of the foil and its wake. By developing a new analytical model, this research accurately predicts the energy input to the second foil, with a high degree of accuracy. This research has significant implications for the design and optimization of future ocean energy systems using oscillating foil turbines.

We've developed a new method to determine the real-time motion of a quark
directly from lattice QCD data. This approach uses Bayesian estimation to
calculate the real-time propagator and identifies the most probable solution
within the constraints of statistical uncertainty and symmetries. To test
its effectiveness, we analyzed the quark's Brownian motion in a hot, non-interacting
gluonic environment and a more complex scenario with non-interacting gluons.
The results show that our method successfully extracts the quantum dynamics
from the lattice data and are consistent with the expectations of a dissipative
theory.

We investigate the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island, focusing on how it's influenced by applied voltage and magnetic fields. In our study, we use a unique method where the quantum dot functions as a sensor to measure gates, enabling us to measure the impact of a finite applied voltage and magnetic field on the quantum dot's conductance. Our results show that a finite applied voltage significantly alters the charge-tunneling resonance, particularly by introducing an additional energy barrier. Furthermore, our experiment demonstrates that even weak magnetic fields can cause a substantial shift in resonance when the quantum dot is strongly coupled to the island, resulting in a hybridized ground state. These findings provide valuable insights into the mechanisms driving charge-tunneling, which is essential for harnessing the phenomenon to create quantum bits in hybrid electron devices.

Developing effective drugs with specific targets is a significant challenge in the field of modern pharmaceutical research. Existing generative models for drug discovery often require extensive computational resources to generate candidates, which can lead to a notable decrease in accuracy over time. In contrast, we introduce Energy-driven Generative Models (EdGMs), a novel approach that learns to produce sequences with lower binding affinity over time. Our EdGMs employ a unique neural network architecture that incorporates an energy function, allowing them to generate candidate sequences with higher specificity for given targets while achieving a faster convergence rate than existing models. Through rigorous testing on two benchmark datasets, our EdGMs demonstrate superior performance over leading baselines in terms of both precision and convergence speed.

The Graph Structure Representation, widely used in logic and computer science since the 1980s, has become a standard for designing algorithms that traverse graph data. Although graphs are valuable, they can be difficult to manipulate due to their diverse set of operations. One solution is to embed additional data within graphs, a technique commonly employed in database systems. We propose a novel method in this study. By incorporating a token-based component, our new data structure enhances graph functionality, making it possible to create interactive applications. By integrating the Geometry of Interaction, our new data structure allows for interactive graph manipulation without affecting in-place updates. We demonstrate the potential of our approach by implementing a web-based tool that utilizes our data structure to provide a user-friendly interface.

The Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) exhibits distinct areas with different properties, particularly in its outer regions, which are influenced by the smaller Magellanic Cloud, situated 180 kiloparsecs away. A comprehensive analysis of the LMC's outer regions, incorporating data from the $V$-band photometry and proper motion measurements from the VISTA Magellanic Cloud survey, has been conducted. This study isolates the LMC's background, comprising stars not associated with the cloud, and identifies distinct populations within the LLMC and WLMC, distinguished by their proper motion and metallicity. A comparison of the LLMC's proper motion distribution with those of the SMC and other dwarf galaxies in the Magellanic Clouds group reveals a similar pattern, indicating a past close encounter between the LMC and the SMC. Furthermore, the investigation examines the effects of the SMC on the LMC, focusing on the spatial and temporal variations of the SMC's influence, which is found to be more pronounced in the LMC's outer regions, particularly in the north-western quadrant.

A deep learning approach is proposed for detecting power theft in smart grids, specifically using AMI networks. A new system combines an extended time-based model with a customized loss function, and a novel loss function is introduced. This function incorporates the Bayesian optimization of hyper-parameters using tree-based Gaussian processes, and a novel tree structure is presented to improve optimization efficiency.
