Through experiments using simulated data, the proposed system is shown to outperform traditional methods in terms of accuracy and computational speed, and the new loss function is found to achieve lower error rates in training.

Compact surfaces have a rich topological structure defined by their covering maps, forming a complete lattice. For each graph defined on a surface, there's an associated graph lattice consisting of refined coverings of the surface. This paper explores how every compact surface graph can be represented as a poset of fine coverings on the surface. This representation mirrors the relationship between such graphs and full graphs on the surface. Additionally, it categorizes the posets of finite graphs on surfaces and identifies specific properties for surface graphs whose poset is complete.

The lifetimes of $Xi^{0}_{c}$ and $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ baryons are measured through the semileptonic decay process $\Xi^{0}_{c}^{*} \rightarrow \Xi^{0}_{c} \pi^{0} \mu^{3}$ and $\Omega^{0}_{c} \rightarrow \Omega^{0}_{c} \pi^{0} \mu^{3}$ respectively. These decays produce the final states $\Xi^{0}_{c} \rightarrow p K^{-} K^{+}$ and $\Omega^{0}_{c} \rightarrow \bar{K}^{*0} \bar{K}^{*0} K^{-} K^{+}$. Using 6 inverse femtobarns of pp collision data collected at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV by the LHCb detector, the results show a lifetime for $Xi^{0}_{c}$ of 7.22 ps, with an error margin of 42 times the size of the measurement, and a lifetime for $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ of 1.33 ps, with an error margin of 21 times the size of the measurement.

This paper introduces an innovative, swift, and precise clustering technique for hyperspectral images based on subspace learning, incorporating a novel regularization method for spectral regression. The proposed approach, SRSC, combines spectral feature reduction with subspace learning and clustering methods while ensuring that the resulting model adheres to spectral constraints. The technique begins by utilizing an improved spectral feature selection method to generate a set of informative spectral bands. Next, it applies spectral regression to obtain low-dimensional data and performs subspace learning while utilizing an optimization method to ensure that the resulting model aligns with spectral properties. The technique then identifies optimal clustering results utilizing the spectral similarity constraint. Experimental evaluations on three hyperspectral images revealed that SRSC outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness.

The complexity of simulating Arctic sea ice deformation is due to the uneven snow cover it accumulates. To simplify this challenge, researchers use a basic model that accounts for the uneven distribution of snow cover by creating undulating ridges on the sea ice. This simplified model accurately recreates the distribution of snow topography on undeformed sea ice when subjected to a specific range of horizontal scales. However, it falls short when analyzing scales beyond a specific threshold, at which point it fails to capture the emergence of a distinct sea ice height function. Further analysis reveals that this limitation arises from the simplified model neglecting the effects of wind-generated shear on the horizontal distribution of snow cover.

We theoretically investigate the quantum Zeno effect on the elastic scattering of ultracold molecules by a cold atom in a harmonic trap.  A distinguishable atom-molecule system is modeled using a pseudopotential interaction, and we apply a dynamic non-selective perturbation to suppress inelastic transitions.  Our results show that the quantum Zeno effect is most effective in strongly coupling regimes, and we apply this to a harmonic trap with a magnetic field oscillating at a frequency much higher than the molecular transition frequency.  Notably, the effect is more pronounced in spin-polarized molecules, and we validate our findings using a time-dependent Schrödinger equation solver for numerical verification.

This research introduces a novel It\^o-Langevin dynamics model that utilizes a non-extensive statistical approach to achieve a more realistic thermodynamic interpretation. It is demonstrated that solutions to the associated Fokker-Planck equation produce the probability density functions for the system in question. Additionally, the paper provides a detailed comparison between the properties of this novel model and those of the traditional Gaussian-Boltzmann model.

A novel class of topological phases, referred to as Weyl semimetals, is characterized by the existence of Weyl nodes with distinct three-dimensional properties in momentum space. These nodes are stable due to the absence of degeneracy with other nodes. The research has demonstrated the possibility of creating a four-dimensional Weyl semimetal within a medium exhibiting optical three-dimensional structure. This was achieved by applying a laser with a two-dimensional periodic pattern to a semimetal, thereby inducing a four-dimensional Dirac nodal line. The application of a weak magnetic field resulted in the separation of the line into discrete Weyl nodes, while a stronger field caused the nodes to merge and lose their three-dimensional stability.

The rise of blockchain technology has led to a growing interest in decentralized computing services. However, existing cloud platforms are limited by their reliance on centralised infrastructure, which hinders their ability to provide fair and transparent computing services. To address this issue, we propose a decentralized computing protocol, Marvel DC, which leverages a blockchain platform to enable fair and transparent computing services. By utilizing a multi-stakeholder consensus method, Marvel DC ensures the reliability of its infrastructure, while a reward-compatible mechanism incentivizes miners to participate, resulting in high network throughput and fairness. To assess its effectiveness, we conducted a series of simulations and case studies, which demonstrate Marvel DC's ability to provide secure, transparent, and efficient cloud services.

A significant hurdle in 3D compression is determining the optimal compression ratio, as no universally accepted quality metrics exist. To address this issue, we present a new metric that provides a comprehensive, multi-faceted assessment of 3D geometry and color by combining three distinct measures. These measures capture spatial characteristics, color patterns, and visual distinctiveness, enabling a more nuanced evaluation of 3D point clouds and colors. Subsequently, we develop a practical application of this metric in the form of a rate-control mechanism for 3D point cloud compression, thereby allowing users to achieve desired quality levels. To validate the effectiveness of our method, extensive testing was conducted using various point cloud datasets, yielding results that demonstrated superior performance over existing techniques.

In holography, researchers have employed a method to map the phase of QCD by analyzing the thermodynamic properties of the BTZ black hole. This method reveals the presence of the first-order phase transition between the confinement and deconfinement phases. The technique can be utilized to determine other key properties of the deconfinement phase, including its chiral critical point. The holographic model indicates the occurrence of the chiral first-order transition at lower temperatures than previously suggested by lattice calculations.

Knee joint abnormalities can be detected using MRI scans, but the manual process of examining these scans is time-consuming, costly, and unreliable. To address this, machine learning methods can be applied to MRI data to automate the assessment. However, MRI data presents challenges due to its complex and variable 3D structure, as well as the limited availability of annotated data. To overcome these issues, we introduce a novel approach, slice-based self-supervised learning (SB-SSL), which leverages data augmentation to create new, artificial MRI slices from real ones. This allows for the creation of self-supervised models that can be combined with a supervised model to improve its performance. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results in MRI-based knee joint anomaly classification, with a notable improvement in the Dice score of 4.2% for the OASIS dataset.

This study introduces a new approach to generating new typesfaces from limited examples, focusing on capturing the unique style features of each typeface. Traditionally, typeface generation techniques have analyzed the overall composition of characters rather than their local details. We address this by employing a deep neural network that combines multiple local shape predictors to generate high-quality typefaces. The predicted shapes are combined into a single character through a learned transformation network. To refine the network's ability to distinguish between typefaces, we incorporate additional regularizers that prevent the model from overfitting to local features, and a style-based loss function to encourage the model to learn the unique style features of each typeface. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing its ability to generate new typefaces from just 10-20 examples, revealing superior results compared to a baseline method.

In equilibrium, a chiral fluid's pressure remains unchanged despite the presence of non-zero shear viscosity, which is a sign of its anomalous nature. This study delves into the effects of transverse heat currents and the Pontryagin index on the pressure and shear stress of the chiral fluid. The research reveals that these currents introduce a new mechanism of shear stress that is connected to the chiral chemical potential, which is a measure of the chiral anomaly. At a constant temperature, the chiral fluid's pressure changes due to the chiral anomaly when the chemical potential is non-constant, resulting in a modified Gibbs-Duheim equation. This relationship holds for fluids with non-constant volumes, classifying them as anisotropic gases.

This paper presents a novel approach within the context of adaptive video streaming, aimed at enhancing user experience in real-time. To achieve this, a novel method has been developed that utilizes a digital twin-based framework. Differing from the conventional approach of utilizing historical data, this framework utilizes real-time network traffic data to predict future network conditions, thereby enabling the improvement of video quality. The proposed method utilizes the predicted network traffic data to determine the optimal video quality by utilizing a reinforcement learning-based algorithm. The primary contributions of this paper include: 1) a novel digital twin-based framework for adaptive video streaming; 2) a novel algorithm for predicting network traffic data; 3) a novel algorithm for optimizing video quality based on the predicted network traffic data. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach can improve user experience by increasing video quality.

In order to identify neutrinos from cosmogenic neutrons, the KM3NeT detector employs a method called double-waterfall reconstruction. This technique enables the detection of muons traversing the surrounding water column and in turn, neutrinos are identified by their absence of muon tracks within the detector. Double-waterfall analysis is particularly effective in distinguishing neutrinos from muons, which often produce coincidental tracks within the detector, resulting in a significant rate of false positives. This article outlines the double-waterfall reconstruction method used for the KM3NeT detector's ARCA sub-array.

The study examines space-time statistics of solutions to the focusing periodic NLS equation with additive space-time white noise, given by:
$$
\mathrm{d}u(t)= \mathrm{e}^{\frac{1}{2} B} \mathrm{V}(u) \mathrm{d}t - \mathrm{e}^{\frac{1}{2} B} \Delta \mathrm{d} \mathbb{W}(t).
$$
Here, $\mathrm{V}$ is a smooth function of periodized space, and it's assumed that $\mathrm{V}$ meets a specific positivity condition related to the Sobolev norm of $u$. The research aims to derive the joint space-time statistics of the associated Cauchy problem, specifically focusing on determining joint space-time moments of the solution, and it achieves this by combining the conservation of energy and a novel "interpolation" method for estimating moments. The method is novel and independent of the traditional method based on the Ito formula.

Ensuring real-time communication across mobile edge computing systems and 5G networks necessitates efficient data transmission over multiple wireless links. The stochastic nature of these links, where data loss is possible, necessitates a combination of forward error correction (FEC) codes and scheduling decisions. The optimal FEC code and schedule depend on the fading link matrices and the target real-time deadline. The proposed joint scheduling and coding approach efficiently utilizes multiple wireless links to meet strict deadlines, achieving this with significantly reduced computational complexity compared to existing methods. The proposed method, which involves a simple linear scheduling policy and a low-complexity FEC code, achieves near-optimal performance while meeting stringent latency requirements.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a significant challenge to our current understanding of star formation and supernovae. A recent study suggests that the initial mass required for supernovae to occur in the vicinity of the supermassive black hole is unfeasibly high, prompting an investigation into the potential formation of Sgr A East from a nearby star. Using a detailed stellar dynamics model, researchers simulated the trajectory of a high-mass star approaching the black hole, estimating the likelihood of a supernova based on stellar evolution theory. The results indicate that the supernova probability is consistent with existing estimates and suggests that the star responsible for the supernova likely originated from the globular cluster Arches.

A principle known as Lepton flavor universality in semileptonic decays implies that lepton flavor does not affect decay rates. Assessments of this principle by the BaBar and Belle experiments have shown compatibility with the predictions of the Standard Model using charged current decays of B-mesons, but there's a discrepancy with the same principle in neutral current decays of B and K mesons. I will summarize current understanding of Lepton flavor universality tests in semileptonic decays of B-mesons, highlighting recent updates on key measurements in semileptonic decays of B and K mesons.

This paper outlines our system developed for the DISRPT2021 Shared Task, which targets three key tasks in discourse analysis: identifying discourse segments, categorizing segment relationships, and locating connectives between them. Our system is grounded in a robust approach to segmenting the discourse, employs pre-trained models to categorize relationships, and adopts an approach involving both pattern-based features and pre-trained models for detecting connectives. Our system's performance excelled in two categories: discourse segmentation, with high accuracy rates of 0.95 and 0.94 for two datasets respectively, and connective detection, with high accuracy rates of 0.63 and 0.64 for two datasets respectively. Furthermore, our results show high accuracy rates of 0.77, 0.80, and 0.63 for segment relationship categorization using two datasets respectively.

The upcoming 6G network will rely heavily on shared infrastructure to meet demands for low latency, high reliability, and environmental sustainability. Clear infrastructure sharing, which builds upon traditional sharing models, allows for the sharing of clear information. However, this approach requires a secure and trusted framework. To address this need, we propose BEAT, a blockchain-enabled system for securing shared infrastructure. BEAT provides protection for each participant, ensuring fair cooperation through a decentralized, permissioned blockchain network. To optimize performance, it leverages off-the-shelf blockchain technologies tailored to BEAT's requirements. Specifically, BEAT utilizes a lightweight, permissioned Hyperledger Fabric blockchain network, which provides fast transaction processing and efficient smart contract management. To further enhance performance, we introduce a joint optimization framework that minimizes the overhead of smart contract execution and transaction processing. To validate the feasibility of BEAT, we conducted a simulation study using the network calculus framework, which confirms that BEAT achieves significant transaction processing speeds, outperforming non-blockchain approaches by up to threefold.

The Okubo-Weiss criterion is a geometric condition that identifies unstable regions within 2D incompressible hydrodynamic flows by examining the complex potential's derivative, or equivalently the vorticity-magnitude vector's curl. We have expanded this concept to magnetohydrodynamics, incorporating magnetic effects and a generalized criterion based on a vorticity-magnitude vector with an added magnetic component.

Lee-Wick theories incorporate negative energy Lee-Wick fields that evade the Pauli exclusion principle by exploiting their dynamic nature rather than spin. The resulting Lee-Wick thermodynamics is characterized by unique properties including a reversal of the first law of thermodynamics. In this study, we explore the effects of Lee-Wick fields on the early universe, specifically focusing on Lee-Wick fields coupled with the standard model Higgs field. We find that their negative energy status doesn't necessarily imply Lee-Wick thermodynamics is always valid. Instead, it's contingent on a specific relationship between the Higgs field's mass and the Lee-Wick field's level number, with only a particular range of values meeting this requirement. Once this range is exceeded, Lee-Wick thermodynamics no longer applies. Interestingly, this condition is satisfied during the early universe's inflationary and radiation-dominated phases but fails towards the present day. As a result, the law of black hole mechanics is violated at our time, potentially offering a novel method for detecting Lee-Wick fields in the future.

The objective of image style transfer is typically achieved by mapping input photographs into a desired style using a style dictionary. However, conventional approaches are often plagued by an imbalance between the generated image's content and style, leading to an unrealistic outcome. In contrast, we introduce a Transformer-based framework called StyTr$^2$, designed to achieve seamless image style transfer without the need for explicit feature alignment between the source and the reference image. The proposed method utilizes a style transformer to selectively extract the most relevant style features from the reference image and a content transformer to preserve the details of the source image. The style and content transformers are jointly trained using two distinct objectives. The experimental results demonstrate that StyTr$^2$ surpasses existing techniques in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, particularly in complex cases involving significant content and style differences.

The Landauer principle establishes the minimum energy required to erase information, but its optimal application remains unclear. Our research demonstrates that a constant dissipation rate in linear quasistatic processes is indeed the most efficient method by utilizing the geometric concept of thermodynamic length. An experimental approach has been developed to measure the dissipation in bit erasure through the use of a voltage source with adjustable slope. Our results confirm that a process with a constant dissipation rate corresponds to the shortest total path length in a double-well potential system, thereby validating the geometric interpretation of the Carnot cycle.

The fourth generation of quarks, known as T-quarks, are proposed as potential explanations for the discrepancy between the predicted and measured Higgs boson's mass. A numerical analysis of pair production of T-quarks at an electron-positron collider, focusing on single-generation scenarios, has been conducted. The study considers both left- and right-chiral T-quarks and investigates their production and detection rates, as well as their decay patterns. It also examines the impact of various detector efficiencies and backgrounds on the signal. The results suggest that a 10-TeV electron-positron collider could detect T-quarks with masses up to 2.4 TeV and up to 2.5 TeV if their couplings to the top quark are not very weak.

This research examines the stability of a non-uniform, linear fluid in the presence of a persistent acoustic field, where acoustic waves continuously travel in one direction. We have discovered that the combination of the fluid's linear flow and the acoustic field generates a specific wave-like disturbance, known as the Benjamin--Feir instability, when the acoustic waves travel faster than the fluid. This instability arises from a resonance effect, where certain wave frequencies interact with the acoustic waves and amplify a certain type of wave, known as the Rossby wave, resulting in the fluid's instability. Our analysis has also shown that the combination of the fluid's linear flow and the stationary acoustic field can produce a different type of instability when the acoustic waves travel slower than the fluid. We have further investigated the effects of the fluid's non-linearity and found that the acoustic waves can trigger a type of instability, known as the Benjamin--Feir instability, even when the fluid is uniform.

We've developed a weighted shift framework on the roots of a generalized directed semi-tree, and our method allows for a straightforward and efficient decomposition of weighted shifts that are a product of the shift and a diagonal multiplication, where the shift is based on a tree with a finite degree at every vertex. Furthermore, our results indicate that any subhomogeneous weighted shift on a tree can be broken down in this way, and a key step in our process involves transforming the weighted shift into a weighted shift of this product type. To achieve this, we also introduced the concept of a directed forest, and our approach to creating this transformation relies heavily on a diagrammatic and combinatorial method.

We've conducted a comprehensive analysis of the interaction between an ultra-intensity gamma-ray flash and high-Z target, with the latter being a 100-micrometer thick gold plate. Our study considered the effect of the gold plate's density and the beam's transverse size on the outcome, using a 100 J, 100 fs pulse at 400 nm to generate the gamma-ray flash. The results revealed that a single shot produces approximately 10^14 electron-positron pairs and 10^9 nuclei in the target, with the latter consisting of atoms with half-lives between 18.5 seconds and 80 years.

Event recognition in videos involves recognizing the actions taking place and their associated meanings in a given setting. To address this challenge, we developed a multi-modal approach for event recognition that integrates visual and linguistic elements. This method utilizes a graph convolutional neural network to process the dynamic interactions between the visual and linguistic modalities. To enhance the model's performance, we suggest applying several modifications to the graph convolutional neural network. Firstly, we suggest utilizing a diverse array of gates to dynamically select information from local and global graph neighborhoods, thereby improving the model's ability to capture long-range dependencies. Furthermore, we propose assigning varying importances to the edges in the graph, based on their visual and linguistic features, to effectively capture the complex relationships between these modalities. Experimental results demonstrate that the modified model outperforms the conventional graph convolutional neural network on event recognition tasks, showcasing the potential of these innovations in improving the performance of graph convolutional neural networks in event recognition tasks.

A Bayesian model for the relationship between an unknown true value and observed data is considered. This relationship is represented as a linear transformation followed by a noise addition. Error-in-variable regression can be applied when both the true value and the original variable are known, often relying on Bayesian principles to handle the issues that arise. A Bayesian model for regression analysis was presented by Carvalho and West (201, 2005). Geometric ergodicity of the associated Markov chain sampling method (Gibbs sampler) is proven in this paper for a large family of prior distributions. This includes both normal-tau and normal-exponential-covariance distributions as special cases. Additionally, the corresponding results are extended to a regression model where independent identically distributed errors are not present.

We introduce a novel algorithm that effectively controls and optimizes the regulation of interconnected multi-qubit systems to achieve the highest possible precision in detecting tiny magnetic changes. This algorithm involves a real-time analysis of the system's underlying dynamics, the application of optimal control theory to determine the most suitable Hamiltonian for maximum sensitivity, and implementation of robust control methods to ensure stability in the presence of minor deviations in the system parameters. This algorithm has been successfully tested on a specific system consisting of three interacting qubits and yielded impressive results: it enhanced the system's detection capability by a factor of 12.5 times relative to uncontrolled regulation, and by a factor of 2.5 times when compared to a less complex but less robust control strategy.

This study explores the use of the Krylov subspace method for solving nonlinear dynamical systems with random disturbances. The proposed approach uses the Galerkin-Petrov method to approximate system solution functions, which are derived from snapshots of numerical solutions to the PDEs. To enhance accuracy, we incorporate a compression phase and employ a multi-kernel technique to handle non-affine system functions using a least-squares method. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the Krylov subspace method in approximating solution functions to high accuracy, with error decay rates influenced by the regularity of the noise.

This research develops mathematical models to predict how waves travel through disordered media, accounting for the way light is absorbed when the wave is very strong. By simplifying a complex nonlinear wave equation into two equations, which describe the lower and upper parts of a wave sequence, researchers can analyze how the wave propagates through the medium. The lower equation involves a specific way of combining terms to describe the absorption of light, while the upper equation includes additional terms that model how the wave affects itself as it travels. The study shows that in certain cases, where the wave is not very strong, the wave's behavior can be described using a single equation with a combination of linear and nonlinear terms, while in very strong cases, the wave's behavior can be described using a single equation with a combination of linear terms. The paper also includes a way to calculate how the wave's behavior changes as it travels through the medium, which can be applied to the case where the wave's strength is very high.

Recent breakthroughs in deep reinforcement learning have led to significant achievements in areas such as robotics and game playing, yet the developed models often produce unpredictable outcomes for critical applications like self-driving vehicles. Although research has focused on creating agents that achieve desired objectives, the study of interpretability in these areas remains relatively underdeveloped. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of interpretable reinforcement learning methods, aiming to distinguish them from unsupervised and supervised techniques. It systematically categorizes these methods into three primary groups based on the underlying principles and mathematical frameworks, followed by a detailed discussion of their practical applications. The ultimate goal of this survey is to provide a unified framework for interpretability research in reinforcement learning, facilitating a deeper understanding of these methods and their practical uses.

This research introduces algebraic representations and semantics for the logic $G_0^N \times C$, which combines the propositional parts of the Grzegorzyk logic with positive Boolean algebra connectives. The study also extends to a multi-variable logic, known as the multi-variable Grzegorzyk lattice-valued logics, and examines the potential of its logic-based approach in reasoning about fixed-point processes in lattice-valued distributed systems.

For a Gaussian process, $G_t$, in the space of functions $C^{p}$ where $p$ is at least three half times the square root of $2$, the Wiener chaos decomposition of its signature sequence $\mathbb{G}$ includes terms that go up to $\ell = 2p$. It's known that the Wiener chaos decomposition is uniquely determined by its restriction to $[0,t]$ as $G_t$ varies. We show that the sequence of $G$ at $t=1$ can be used to determine all terms up to $\ell$ in the Wiener chaos decomposition of the signature sequence $\mathbb{G}_t$ provided that $\ell$ is at least two. We then extend this result to a Gaussian process that is almost surely smooth by demonstrating that the sequence of $G$ at $t=1$ can be used to establish a one-to-one correspondence between the Wiener chaos decompositions of $\mathbb{G}_t$ for $t$ in the interval from one to one plus some $\delta$ and the interval from one plus some $\delta$ to one plus some $\delta$.

This study examines the effectiveness of millimeter-wave (mmWave) cellular networks in maintaining communication quality by analyzing how line-of-sight (LOS) and non-LOS (NLOS) connections impact the availability of network services. By utilizing the Rayleigh fading model and incorporating a 3GPP urban outdoor channel model, we develop analytical methods to evaluate localization performance in both LOS and NLOS scenarios. Focusing on two prevalent localization algorithms, least squares and multistage multivariant recursive (MSMR), we investigate the root-mean-square error (RMSE) of these methods to determine the network's localization accuracy. The results show that a network's ability to maintain a low RMSE is heavily dependent on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and the density of user equipment (UE). Notably, a high UE density is crucial for maintaining a low RMSE, especially in LOS scenarios, but may be less critical in NLOS scenarios. Additionally, our findings suggest that MSMR outperforms LS in terms of RMSE, and that a moderate UE density can achieve similar localization accuracy to a high-density network at a higher SNR. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that a high UE density can compensate for lower SNR in maintaining a low RMSE, but at the cost of increased power consumption.

We provide a distinct demonstration of achieving Bose-Einstein condensation in an interacting Bose gas, one that operates within the mean-field framework of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation. By considering a fully coupled system of equations for the density and phase of the gas, we show that in the thermodynamic limit, a non-degenerate condensate forms at the ground state energy level. This result provides an alternative to existing methods of obtaining BEC using the Gross-Pitaevskii equation and is compatible with them.

The goal of image inpainting is to recover missing regions in images by processing partial input data. This challenging task typically requires precise pixel-level predictions and a thorough understanding of image details. Recent advancements in deep learning-based methods have yielded impressive results, surpassing traditional techniques in certain aspects. However, most deep learning models are designed to produce low-resolution images for low-resolution representations. Furthermore, they are less effective when faced with intricate details in high-resolution images. To address these limitations, our proposed method employs a two-tiered deep learning approach that combines low-resolution and high-resolution representations to tackle complex image restoration tasks. The model consists of two stages: a low-resolution encoder that extracts coarse image features and a high-resolution decoder that generates detailed image information. To facilitate high-resolution processing, our approach utilizes a novel high-resolution feature extraction module that extracts high-resolution features from local neighborhoods. Additionally, a two-tiered generator is designed to process low-resolution and high-resolution features separately. The model is trained using a novel image reconstruction loss function that combines both low-resolution and high-resolution images for effective image recovery. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in image inpainting tasks, particularly in producing high-resolution results.

In the context of structured thresholding bandit problems, we investigate issue-dependent arms with specific structures, such as matrix, graph, or hypergraph, where adjacent arms share a common reward. Our research focuses on two new problem variants: priority thresholding bandits, where arms are thresholded based on their associated rewards, and interval thresholding bandits, where arms are grouped into intervals and only the last element in each interval is considered in the thresholding process. We propose UCBvP and UCBvi algorithms, which offer improved regret bounds for these two settings. Our algorithm for priority thresholding bandits achieves a time-dependent regret that, under specific conditions, grows at a rate of O(\sqrt(m T log(m T)) / m), and for interval thresholding bandit it achieves a time-dependent regret that grows at a rate of O(\sqrt{T log log T}), where m represents the size of the thresholding groups. Our research also includes a comprehensive study of issue-dependent arms, where we categorize and compare different settings, such as issue-dependent arms with static and dynamic arms, and provide a unified analysis of issue-dependent arms, using a new notion of regret. Our results show that issue-dependent arms significantly impact regret analysis, especially in the context of structured thresholding bandits.

This paper delves into the techniques used in and provides a comprehensive overview of the associated sections from the original article. Furthermore, it expands on the concept by exploring several other applications and related ideas.

We show that K\"ahler metrics on certain complete self-dual manifolds of non-negative curvature are preserved under a specific flow, and remain smooth in all dimensions and time over the entire Riemannian manifold.

We establish the existence of the integrated density of states and its derivative for any vortex configuration in a disordered two-dimensional superfluid, yielding an exact expression for the derivative in terms of Bessel functions. Our analysis shows that as the system size increases, the distribution of vortex pairs in a disordered two-dimensional superfluid displays Coulomb scattering behavior, characterized by a power-law density of states derivative, featuring a logarithmic divergence. We confirm this result using numerical methods and further investigate the distribution of low-magnitude vortex pairs in a random potential, finding that as their magnitude tends towards zero, their distribution follows a square-root pattern, with a width scaling inversely with their magnitude.

Public perceptions of artificial intelligence, particularly in emerging technologies, can greatly influence policy and societal acceptance. Our study conducted a survey of over 10,000 people across 8 countries to explore how individuals view artificial intelligence, and the results reveal mixed sentiments. According to our research, nearly nine out of ten individuals trust their governments to manage AI development, but only a small fraction, around 10-15%, believe their governments are doing so effectively. Our data indicates that most people have high hopes for the potential of AI to improve their lives but also have significant concerns regarding its safety and ethics, and this dual perspective is consistent across all countries surveyed. Our findings suggest that people's perceptions of AI's benefits and risks will shift as more people engage with and gain experience with the technology.

Researchers have conducted a statistical analysis of the decay $\Xi_c^0$ utilizing data from the $pp$ collisions at 7 TeV, which were recorded using the LHCb detector between 2010 and 2012, amounting to 1.0 $\fb^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. The investigation focused on the $\Xi_c^0\to\pi^-\Lambda_c^+$ decay mode, which was isolated by identifying the $\Lambda_c^+$ baryon through its decay into $\pi^+ K^-$. The measured branching fraction of the $\Xi_c^0$ decay, relative to $\Xi_c^0\to p K^- \bar{\Xi}_c^0$, was determined to be $0.398 \pm 0.025 \pm 0.025 \pm 0.044$. The given uncertainties include the statistical fluctuation, a specific relative uncertainty and a correction for branching fraction uncertainties of the $\Xi_c^0\to p K^- \bar{\Xi}_c^0$ and $\Lambda_c^+\to p K^- K^+$ decays, respectively. The $\Xi_c^0\to \pi^-\Lambda_c^+$ decay mode has been identified as a sensitive probe for testing the Standard Model through the first measurement of the branching ratio for the $\Xi_c^0\to \pi^-\Lambda_c^+$ decay mode.

This study presents equations that link fixed points of product operators to those of individual operators and examines the existence of these linked fixed points under generalized Lipschitz conditions in Banach algebras. The outcomes have practical applications in solving first-order nonlinear functional equations with continuous, coercive, and quadratic derivatives in the context of Banach algebras.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms have become a leading solution for training deep neural network-based policies. However, they frequently get stuck in a situation where the policy model gets stuck in a local minimum, resulting in slow convergence. This issue can be addressed by exploring other machine learning techniques, such as those based on gradient descent. A technique called Hamiltonian Monte Carlo has already shown its potential in overcoming some limitations of neural networks. This study demonstrates that Hamiltonian Monte Carlo can be used to improve the actor-critic algorithm by making it more robust to bad local minima and improving its convergence speed. This improved actor-critic algorithm was tested on a range of benchmarks including Atari games and the MuJoCo robotics environment, and it was found that the resulting policy models were not only less prone to getting stuck in a local minimum, but also showed improved performance compared to the original actor-critic algorithm.

We investigate a quantum version of the Van der Waals equation within a specific three-level atom-chain-cavity framework, which includes interactions between the atoms and the cavity in addition to cavity dissipation. The study reveals that this model can be described using three control parameters: the interaction strength, dissipation rate, and cavity frequency. A detailed examination of the joint spectral density indicates the presence of four distinct phases: a quantum superposition state, a quantum magnet, a superradiant magnet, and a quantum condensate. The quantum magnet and the superradiant magnet are found to exist in a range of the dissipation and interaction parameter space, with the latter transitioning into the former when the dissipation strength is decreased. The quantum magnet is characterized by long-range order in the form of chiral correlations, while the superradiant magnet is distinguished by the presence of a chiral order parameter. A more detailed examination of the quantum magnet is carried out, which is found to exist in a tricritical line within the phase transition between the quantum magnet and the quantum condensate.

In many real-world applications, multiple agents must cooperate to achieve common objectives, yet the field of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) remains underdeveloped. Our research focuses on developing efficient algorithms for cooperative tasks, where agents must work together to achieve common objectives. We've found that transferring knowledge from experienced agents to newly introduced agents can be particularly effective, as it promotes efficient learning and adaptability in dynamic environments. Our proposed algorithm, MACMATL, enables seamless knowledge transfer by matching new agents with experienced ones, and uses a sophisticated level-based approach to determine each agent's contribution to the overall task. Our experimental results demonstrate the superiority of MACMATL compared to state-of-the-art baselines in various cooperative environments.

The potential of particle robotics in addressing complex tasks such as search and rescue operations has been largely unexploited due to current limitations in robot design. Our proposed novel robot, called the SwarmOdy, features a unique design where multiple actuators are distributed across its body, each capable of exerting a force on a single object. Unlike previous particle robots, SwarmOdy can perform both navigation and object manipulation. Our research presents a deep reinforcement learning framework that enables SwarmOdy to learn from raw visual data, develop a navigation policy, and adapt to dynamic environments. The proposed framework demonstrates the robot's ability to acquire complex skills, such as navigating through cluttered spaces and manipulating objects, and achieves comparable performance to that of a traditional control approach.

Using the 8.2 m GREGOR telescope, we conducted a high-priority observation of the atmospheric properties of WASP-31b through near-infrared echelle spectroscopy. Our goal was to verify the presence of potassium in the planet's atmosphere, which previous studies had suggested might be present in small quantities. However, our data show no evidence of potassium or other elements, and the non-detection of neutral potassium specifically sets a 3 sigma upper limit of 2.4 pm eq-part percent. Given the limited resolution of our spectrum, this limit is expected to be conservative and could be further reduced with higher resolution observations in the future.

The concept of HPC as a service through the cloud is still in its early stages, despite the benefits it offers, such as reduced administrative burdens and greater scalability. However, the current cloud infrastructure lacks essential features for delivering truly on-demand computing, with persistent storage and scalable, high-speed data access being two significant shortcomings. The cloud's reliance on NVM-based servers, combined with innovative technologies like FaaS, can overcome these limitations, ultimately revolutionizing the way scientists and researchers utilize HPC as a cloud service.

Understanding human behavior and thought processes is crucial for medical diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Recent advances in neuroimaging technology, specifically functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), have allowed for the collection of detailed data on brain activity. Researchers have developed machine learning models to analyze this data, but there is a major limitation: the lack of labeled fMRI data. To overcome this challenge, a new method called contrastive learning is proposed to learn from multiple individuals' data, without requiring labels. This method leverages population-wide patterns to classify fMRI data, and relies on a graph neural network to model relationships between brain regions. Experiments on large fMRI datasets have shown that this method can achieve high classification accuracy even when there are large individual differences.

This paper explores a type of total quotient subcategory $\mathbf{X}$ in a total additive category $\mathbf{C}$, which is characterized by its closure under some type of epimorphisms in $\mathbf{C}$. This concept is utilized to introduce the "Gauss quotients" of various mathematical structures, such as modules, Lie algebras, and modules over ringoids. The paper also delves into the properties of these Gauss quotients and establishes a relationship between them and existing quotients in these mathematical contexts. A generalization of the Gauss quotient for functors is also presented, which allows for the derivation of Gauss quotients for a range of mathematical structures. The paper further examines the properties of Gauss quotients in various categorical contexts, including the derivation of a fundamental theorem for the Gauss quotient of modules and the development of the dual Gauss quotient for Lie algebras.

Our research has successfully identified and measured the spectral distribution of soft X-ray Cherenkov radiation generated when high-energy electrons interact with thin solid targets made of beryllium and silicon. The observed Cherenkov radiation peaks at a wavelength of approximately 22 nanometers for beryllium and 40 nanometers for silicon. The experimental data were collected and compared to theoretical predictions provided by a Green's function approach that accounts for both Landau and Bethe-Heitler processes. The results show that the measured spectral intensities of the Cherenkov radiation generally match the predicted values, although the measured intensities for beryllium are notably higher than the expected values.

This report presents our system's entries to the ECIR 2021 UCCA Shared Task, focusing on Corefelt annotations for the task. We outline how we processed the input data and describe our systems for argument head prediction and primary UCCA structure creation. We also report our UCCA-based baseline for additional argument enhancements.

Recent studies have utilized weak supervision techniques, such as box annotations, to classify and identify abnormal areas in chest X-rays, minimizing the need for precise masks. A Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework, which considers the entire image as a whole, has proven effective in distinguishing normal and abnormal images. Our research builds upon MIL by introducing a self-supervised approach, Self-DML, which eliminates the need for any labels during the training phase. This is achieved through the incorporation of two trained networks: one for distinguishing normal and abnormal images, and another for distinguishing healthy and abnormal sub-volumes. Our proposed framework, Self-DML, outperforms existing methods in binary and ternary classification tasks, and its performance is comparable to that of weakly supervised approaches when evaluated using the NIH chest X-ray dataset.

In statistical analysis, model selection plays a crucial role, especially when working with limited data samples. A key concept in this process is the concept of divergence, which measures the distance between models. This work introduces a novel model selection approach based on a penalized Hellinger divergence metric that minimizes asymptotic risks while performing well with limited sample sizes. The method is applied to the regression context and its performance is evaluated through simulations and real-world data applications.

The Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence can be expressed through a binary tree of 0 and 1, with its construction determined by a simple replacement rule: flipping the bits of the sequence to its left. Studying the tree's structure, a researcher found that all possible binary motifs of a certain size appear at specific nodes, with this result's proof relying on a combinatorial argument and the sequence's generating function. This result has an interesting connection to another finite-state sequence known as the Fibonacci sequence. It's also shown how this result can be used to count the number of motifs in the more complex Post's correspondence problem, with this result then being compared to a similar result from a different sequence known as the Pufnery sequence.

Dynamic Classifier Selection (DCS) methods choose the most suitable classifier from a set to handle new data points by considering their characteristics. Current methods pick one classifier at a time for each data point, but this approach can be time-consuming. To address this, we propose a new method called Cost-sensitive Hierarchical grouping for Dynamic Classifier Selection (CHGS). CHGS groups similar data points in a tree and chooses the relevant child node, sending it to the most expensive classifier. This allows it to process multiple data points at once and reduce costs. Moreover, CHGS is efficient and can run quickly even with large datasets. In our experiments with 32 datasets, CHGS outperformed other DCS methods in terms of accuracy, cost, and time.

The Tianlai project involves a series of experiments focused on detecting Baryon Acoustic Oscillations and features two telescopes with 1000 and 19 channels respectively. Data management for the project is complicated by the sheer volume of data generated and the need for efficient BAO signal extraction. This signals a shift in focus from previous experiments on which the project has focused, requiring both a consideration of long-term impact and potential re-evaluation of data management approaches common in cosmology research. In light of these demands, a new pipeline was designed from scratch, incorporating a robust architecture and tailored functionality. This paper outlines the data management pipeline used by the Tianlai experiment and assesses its performance based on real-world usage.

To explore potential applications in spintronic devices, we investigate the magnetic properties of finite-size, monolayer vanadium silicenitrides, focusing on their ground states and magnetic moments through density functional theory calculations. We discover that while vanadium silicenitride (VSi2N4) and vanadium silicide (VSi2) exhibit different ground states, both antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic, vanadium silicenitride only exhibits an antiferromagnetic ground state, whereas vanadium silicide exhibits both. Notably, VSi2N4 exhibits an antiferromagnetic ground state, but its magnetic moment is significantly reduced compared to VSi2. Furthermore, VSi2N4 exhibits a high Curie temperature, suggesting its potential for applications in spintronic devices. In contrast, NbSi2N4 remains in a non-magnetic state, but VSi2N4 and VSi2 exhibit magnetic moments that are comparable in magnitude to VSi2, despite differing in their atomic numbers. Consequently, VSi2N4 and VSi2 exhibit magnetic moments that are comparable in magnitude to VSi2, despite the atomic number of nitrogen (N) being less than that of silicon (S).

This work introduces a set of positive-definite functions defined on a metric space with a specific structure, derived from a non-parametric model of spatially correlated data within bounded regions. Our model posits that correlations between locations follow a power-law pattern with modifications tailored to data observed near boundaries. Given the limitations of power-law functions in capturing this behavior, our model provides an alternative solution. As a result, it offers a simpler yet efficient solution to the problem of generating positive-definite functions for data collected in bounded areas.

For a positive semigroup on a finite set with d elements, we investigate the definition of atomicity, which is based on the distribution of cyclic patterns. We then examine the set of atomic subgroup semigroups, determine specific conditions under which every positive semigroup on a set with prime power size 'p^d' exhibits atomic subgroups, and demonstrate that subgroups of the symmetric group S_n can be atomic if and only if they meet a certain condition in their central elements.

The attributable fraction among the exposed, often denoted as AF_e, measures the case incidence that could have been avoided if exposure had been null. It's a key quantity in the quantal regression model, used to assess the causal impact of risk factors like smoking. However, calculating AF_e reliably is complex due to its reliance on incidence among the unexposed, which isn't directly observed. A novel approach is proposed to estimate AF_e by leveraging case description data, where case-level information is available for both the exposed and the unexposed. This includes demographic attributes like age, sex, and smoking status, as well as information on never-exposed individuals' smoking habits. A new method is developed to construct an odds ratio for exposure among cases, denoted as OR_e, and it's used to derive an unbiased estimate of AF_e. This method is based on the weighted odds ratio, specifically OR_e, and it's used to derive an unbiased estimate of AF_e. This method is applied to a dataset of lung cancer cases to demonstrate its reliability in estimating AF_e in the presence of confounding biases.

We extend Bloch's formula to the category of varieties over finite fields, thereby expanding upon the work of Schwede, Steenbergen, and Spasievo, and also build upon the research of Kato and Saito by deriving a Rossetti formula for such varieties. As an application of these findings, we establish the Lefschetz formula within the context of finite fields.

Researchers have analyzed data from 7 TeV proton-proton collisions collected by the LHCb experiment in 2010, amounting to an integrated luminosity of 35 pb^-1. The focus is on various $\Upsilon$(nS) cross-section ratios in five distinct event classes, based on the number of charged particles, both in decay to dimuons and in a two-dimensional differential decay length distribution. The results show that the cross-section ratios of $\Upsilon$(nS) remain consistent across the studied charged particle multiplicity and dimuon production point of view. However, the $\Upsilon$(nS) production is found to be dependent on the dimuon transverse momentum but not on the number of charged particles in the decay production distribution. The dimuon transverse momentum has a significant effect on the production distribution of $\Upsilon$(nS) and on the average decay length within the studied momentum range.

Our analysis delves into the entropic properties of a strongly connected quantum dot, a diode, a capacitor, and an inductor, all in relation to their electromagnetic connections, using the principles of nonequilibrium thermodynamics. We employ entropic port-Hilbert spaces to represent these devices and develop a generalized entropy equation that accounts for the relationships between heat, work, and entropy flows through the systems. Our results show that the minimum entropy generated by each device can be determined by comparing the lengths of vectors in the entropic port-Hilbert spaces. We also examine the effects of external time-varying potentials and electromagnetic coupling strengths on the entropic portraits of these systems.

The Geometric Modulus Principle is a concept introduced by Fuks that describes a boundary value problem for second-order hyperbolic partial differential equations in a complex geometric setting. In this work, we explore a more general formulation of this principle, applicable to holomorphic and harmonic functions within the context of metric spaces. Our development is significant as it expands the scope of the Geometric Modulus Principle, while its practical applications are relatively modest. As an illustration of this expansion, we demonstrate how the broader principle can be utilized to create novel proofs for the convergence of certain series related to holomorphic and harmonic functions on metric graphs.

We have examined the stability of bright solitons within a discrete nonlinear Schrodinger model, which incorporates both dipole-dipole and on-site nonlinear interactions, using a modulational instability approach. The stability analysis revealed that, for a certain range of interaction strengths between sites, the nonlinear bright solitons remain stable. However, when the interaction strengths exceed this range, the solitons become unstable. This instability leads to the rapid growth of radiation fields emanating from the central site, which then spread outward in a ring. Notably, a specific model parameter, the quadratic phase term, significantly influences the stability of these bright solitons, confirming their sensitivity to this variable.

Optimizing problems involving inequalities in logarithmic or exponential terms can be complex, particularly when non-linear constraints are involved. Geometric programming offers an approach to tackle these challenges, initially designed for control systems and signal processing, and has since expanded to other fields. Building on this foundation, we draw inspiration from geometric programming to develop methods for solving non-linear optimization problems. Building a bridge between optimization theory and the study of rational functions, we draw parallels to existing methods for solving similar problems. We demonstrate the practical application of these methods in solving signomial programming problems.

The Teichmuller spaces' actions on the mapping class group have implications in ergodic theory, particularly concerning Teichmuller geodesic dynamics, and contribute to Mod_{g,n}'s role in the global Torelli problem.

Recent advancements in neural radiance fields and neural point fields have led to significant performance improvements in reconstructing detailed 3D avatars from single-user videos. Although existing methods rely on predefined standard templates, they often struggle to accommodate diverse and complex character geometries. This paper proposes PINA, a novel approach for reconstructing customized implicit neural avatars directly from a single RGB-D video, without requiring pre-defined skeletal structures. To address this challenge, PINA employs a dynamic and non-rigid 3D point space, where each point is dynamically assigned to a 3D code. By integrating a dynamic 3D point encoding framework and a customized feature propagation scheme, PINA effectively captures both static and dynamic 3D features across different frames. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that PINA significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of reconstruction accuracy, allowing it to accurately reconstruct complex characters with diverse and dynamic features.

Revealing concealed facial features has a multitude of practical uses, such as enhancing facial recognition in low-quality images and mitigating the effects of lighting conditions. A significant challenge lies in the fact that current face de-occlusion methods fail to accurately reconstruct three-dimensional facial shapes and local details. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that combines a generative competitive network with a 3D morphable model to recover both global and local facial characteristics. To facilitate the recovery of partially obscured facial regions, we introduce a 3D morphable model-based network that incorporates a target face representation, which enables it to search for de-occluded facial regions in a specific area. Additionally, we incorporate a local detail reconstruction module that recovers intricate facial details. To achieve this, we develop a generative competing network that competes with the target face to reconstruct the de-occluded regions, using a combination of discriminative loss and a novel reconstruction loss. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we created a new benchmark consisting of 3D scans of 200 faces with various levels of partial concealment. The results demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses existing approaches in terms of global facial accuracy and local detail recovery.

Intrinsic motivation is a theoretical concept explaining how motivation can be generated from within, allowing an agent to make decisions solely based on personal objectives. This concept has been applied to reinforcement learning, providing a framework that includes a range of different intrinsic motivations, some example outcomes, and a classification system. This study examines the theoretical underpinnings of intrinsically-driven reinforcement learning, its connection to the information-processing theory of motivation, and its potential relationship to the brain's function. It then outlines a basic reinforcement learning architecture, introduces the proposed classification system, and illustrates the diverse range of possible intrinsic motivations, some being task-specific and others being general, along with their potential uses and benefits. This study also identifies areas for further research and proposes test cases for evaluating the proposed framework.

In a multi-agent reinforcement learning environment, we investigate a decentralized policy and state model, where agents interact with their local surroundings, led by a group of decision makers who define the overall network strategy. To achieve cooperation, these leaders must agree on a unified policy throughout the system, which we demonstrate can converge using a iterative communication approach, based on the assumption of complete information sharing among nearby leaders.

This study examined the characteristics of events with two leading jets and a considerable gap in pseudorapidity, using data from proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV, collected 1020 nb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity with the LHCb detector. The data were compared to predictions from the gluon-gluon fusion and quark-gluon fusion models. A notable gap between jets, situated between the rapidity of the leading jet (denoted as Y$_{J1}$) and another jet (denoted as Y$_{J2}$), was observed. The data revealed that the cross-section for the selected events was 261 $\mu$b for the range 5 $\le$ Y$_{J1} <$ 6.0 and 7 $\le$ Y$_{J2} <$ 1.0, with a 1.9 sigma discrepancy from the next-to-leading-order perturbative QCD calculations. Furthermore, the differential cross-section for the minimum bias process in the specified Y$_{J1}$ and Y$_{J2}$ ranges was also calculated and compared to predictions from the same models.

Silicon, an extensively researched element due to its exceptional electronic and mechanical properties, has garnered significant attention following the successful creation of silicene, a low-dimensional silicon structure. Researchers have investigated the thermoelectric potential of penta-silicene, a ring-shaped silicon structure with five atoms in each unit cell, and found it to possess a distinctive phase diagram under ambient conditions, featuring an insulating state at low temperatures and a degenerate Fermi liquid at high temperatures. The latter exhibits unusual transport characteristics, including a large Seebeck coefficient and a significant electrical conductivity, as well as the presence of two distinct charge carriers with opposite signs. Consequently, the figure of merit of penta-silicene appears to be highly dependent on temperature and field conditions, and its optimal performance is achieved at room temperature, with a maximum value of 2.9 at 300 K in direct bandgap configurations.

We investigate the ground and excited state charmonium and bottomonium spectral functions under the influence of a magnetic field and thermal effects using the fractional non-relativistic quark model. The model's efficacy is supported by its success in predicting the masses of various hadrons with precision. The magnetic field's impact is considered through the application of fractional Calogero-type equations, which describe the dynamics of a non-relativistic quark within the quark model. The thermal effects are incorporated by employing the Gaussian approximation to describe the thermal mass correction. Our study reveals that the magnetic field causes the spectral function to broaden. As the temperature increases, the spectral function initially broadens, then splits into two distinct peaks, before merging into a broad peak again. The peak corresponding to the excited state experiences the most significant thermal shift.

We've conducted an extensive analysis of the interactions between dark matter particles and the standard model, specifically for subhalos within galaxies. This study focuses on a simplified model of fermionic dark matter, where particles are restricted from exiting the Earth by a mass difference of at least 5 keV. Using this model, we have made accurate calculations of the resulting scattering cross-sections and applied them to a range of experiments, including neutron star capture, cosmic ray measurements, and old rock samples. We found that a future gravitational wave detector could achieve the most stringent bounds on the cross-sections of fermionic dark matter, exceeding 10^16 eV/cm^2, while existing and forthcoming cosmic ray and rock experiments may reach the level of 10^-14 to 10^-17 eV/cm^2, depending on the specific type of detector and the kinematic parameters of the subhalos involved.

A game model, known as signaling games, is used to study complex interactions in situations where information transfer does not occur in a straightforward manner. Within these games, participants strive to effectively convey their true characteristics to others based on limited and uncertain knowledge. To achieve this, we introduce a novel agent-based model, called sGAL, which learns optimal policies by balancing risk and reward in the face of uncertainty, in real-time and offline. To tackle the challenges posed by learning under uncertainty, sGAL employs reinforcement learning and neural networks to develop strategies that cater to diverse signal scenarios, varying levels of uncertainty, and across multiple agents. Our approach is evaluated across five network-based signaling games, demonstrating significant improvements in agent performance through the use of reinforcement learning.

Reinforcement learning has been widely used in mobile robotics for its ability to handle complex tasks, but its effectiveness can be compromised when data is contaminated during the training process. To address this issue, we present TERP, a reliable outdoor navigation system based on RL, specifically designed for robots operating in unsteady conditions and relying on a limited number of sensors. We propose a new framework, featuring a two-stage approach: a safety-oriented phase to identify potential hazards and an exploration phase to navigate the environment. This framework utilizes a single deep neural network to achieve reliable outdoor planning. We evaluate the performance of our approach through experiments on a mobile robot, focusing on a real-world application involving autonomous navigation foraging tasks in a university campus.

The isotropic dipolar model is a unique ferromagnetic system with anisotropic interactions that exhibits a complex phase diagram with multiple phases. By applying both Landau theory and Monte Carlo simulations, we have derived a comprehensive phase chart for a 3D dipolar model, showing that it undergoes a first-order phase transition from a paramagnetic to a ferromagnetic state. Further analysis revealed the presence of two distinct ferromagnetic phases characterized by non-collinear and collinear spin arrangements, mediated by a first-order phase transition. Our results also indicate that the application of the Ising universality class to the first-order transition may not be entirely accurate.

The goal of this research is to determine the location, shape, and material properties of a conductive object within a uniform electric field generated by a point source. Initially, it's proven that identifying the object's boundaries from the external field is feasible if it's surrounded by a conductive material with uniform conductivity. However, determining both the object's shape and conductivity proves to be challenging as it's linked together by mathematical equations, requiring initial conditions or additional constraints to be uniquely solvable.

The dynamics of magnetic fields in stars is crucial for understanding their evolution and development. We have developed a theoretical framework that calculates the stability of toroidal magnetic fields in stars, which is essential for maintaining axial symmetry. Our study shows that in non-rotating stars, magnetic fields from the dynamo must be highly powerful to prevent instabilities, requiring a certain fraction of the star's energy from being magnetic. However, rotating stars with stable differential rotation exhibit toroidal magnetic fields that remain stable for any intensity, except during brief phases of quenching when the magnetic energy temporarily exceeds the star's energy. We have discovered that in such cases, magnetic fields in rotating stars can remain stable for any strength, provided the quenching duration is significantly shorter than the timescale of magnetic relaxation. Our findings suggest that in stars without a convective core, magnetic fields can maintain axial symmetry, whereas in stars with a convective core, magnetic fields must be highly powerful to sustain the symmetry.

This research delves into the intricate topological and geometric properties of simple one-dimensional networks that serve as their foundational structure. The study begins by examining the intricate patterns of complex one-dimensional networks, which are crucial for the functioning of two-dimensional networks. The research then focuses on the unique topological features of these one-dimensional paths, demonstrating that they have the capability to fully represent the topological properties of two-dimensional networks. The study further explores the geometric characteristics of complex one-dimensional networks, which are found to be highly coordinated in their structural arrangements. The research ultimately identifies the underlying geometric principles, which are found to be regulated by the length of the network and the density of edges that connect its components.

Sparse matrix multiplication and linear solvers are crucial components in numerous scientific and engineering applications. SpMVs serve as a crucial component in iterative methods used to solve complex linear systems. Given that these methods often involve repeated SpMVs, minimizing SpMV execution time is essential to optimize solution time. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of various strategies to enhance the performance of SpMVs, including vectorization techniques, matrix storage formats, and caching efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate the impact of the Strassen algorithm on matrix storage formats and show that formats with varying row column density (RCDS) can lead to significant performance improvements, with improvements of up to 45% achieved in certain cases. Moreover, the Strassen algorithm results in a 10% performance boost for sparse matrices with a high density of rows and columns. Additionally, caching efficiency can lead to a 25% performance gain for highly sparse matrices.

The purpose of this paper is to present a definitive answer to a problem posed by Pang and Wang in 2013 through developing new findings on the sharing of values for meromorphic functions, ultimately providing a comprehensive response to the associated question.

Advancements in AR hardware are creating new opportunities for social interaction to evolve, yet the potential impact on human relationships remains a topic of concern. This study examines how individuals' perceptions of AR use might influence social relationships, specifically by recognizing people's intentions when using their AR-enhanced devices in social settings. To investigate further, we developed HAIR, a head-mounted AR-specific identifier, which we then tested on a crowd-sourced dataset collected over two years, consisting of 177 head-mounted AR device captures from 114 individuals. Our results indicate that HAIR can accurately categorize AR device use across five categories: phone, HMD, and combinations of two, three, or all. Moreover, we found that individuals exhibiting certain behaviors, such as ignoring others, or using multiple devices together, may be perceived as having malicious intentions. These findings suggest that individuals' social behavior is influenced by their AR device use, which in turn can impact how others perceive their intentions.

For Monge-Amp\`ere systems, we've developed a novel class of coupling functions that incorporate multiple Lagrangian systems simultaneously. This innovation allows us to maintain the stability of their interconnected systems and the conservation of the underlying system's structure. Furthermore, our method provides a straightforward and efficient solution technique that utilizes a combination of relaxation and perturbation techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through its application to a complex system involving a 2x2 conservation law and a transport equation, as well as a 1D Euler model. In each instance, our method yields high-quality numerical solutions that compare favorably to existing alternatives.

The way bubbles form and dissolve on electrodes is crucial for understanding various electrochemical processes, yet the influence of convection caused by differences in bubble density remains unclear. This study utilized a high-speed camera to observe the impact of natural convection on bubble growth and dissolution, using both symmetric and asymmetric electrolyte solutions in different tank geometries. The research revealed that these external factors can reduce bubble growth rates and cause unstable fluid motion, leading to bubble detachment from the electrode surface. As a result, the mass transport of species between bubbles and the electrode is significantly affected, which can lead to changes in the concentration of active sites on the electrode surface. This could potentially explain why certain electrolytes are more effective in certain processes, such as the electrolysis of potassium hydroxide in hydrogen fuel cells, as opposed to sodium hydroxide.

A recent study focused on identifying subatomic particles with extended lifetimes using an innovative analysis of photons delayed in their emission. This research utilized data from 13 TeV proton-proton collisions, collected with the CMS detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider for a total of 101 fb^-1 integrated luminosity. To isolate the desired photons, researchers employed techniques that minimized background from other sources, such as charged particles and additional photons. This marked the first evidence of time-dependent fluctuations in photon pairs, indicating that the analysis can detect particles with lifetimes of approximately 1 ns. The findings also placed constraints on the presence of new heavy vector bosons and Z' bosons decaying into photon pairs and on the existence of charginos produced through Higgs-mediated mechanisms.

This study explores the impact of Coulomb interactions within the framework of second-order Dirac semiconductors. We demonstrate that the interactions result in the emergence of a mass term in the effective model. Additionally, a more sophisticated model incorporating the effects of velocity-like dipole terms is presented. Notably, it is found that these dipole terms are significantly more pronounced than those found in similar semiconductor materials lacking Dirac semantics.

One of the most significant obstacles in developing software is creating a design for a data structure that can efficiently support the operations it will support. One effective method to simplify this process is data abstraction, where data structure parameters are abstracted away, allowing designers to focus on operations without specific data considerations. Researchers have developed a method to automatically generate data structure implementations based on abstracted data structure diagrams using a rule-based approach. This study investigates this problem as a planning problem within an answer set programming framework, specifically describing Prolog rules for data structure diagrams and SPAS answers. We will present an example of using this method to generate an implementation for a stack, and discuss its potential applications and limitations, as well as potential extensions to the method.

A novel technique for monitoring and adjusting the position of a microsphere in contact with a gravitational field has been developed, utilizing a magnetic levitation trap combined with optical techniques. By integrating a laser trap and a microsphere with a magnetic levitated harmonic oscillator, researchers have been able to study the interaction between thermal fluctuations, damping, and quantum effects in both the microsphere and the harmonic oscillator. These findings enable the exploration of various test scenarios for alternative theories of gravity, including those with modifications to Newton's law, MOND, and the screening of gravity.

We've identified two new molecules, ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers, namely 1-CC3C5CH and 1-CH3CCCH2C5H, along with the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomer 1-CH2CCCCH, through observations made at the AAT Yebes radio telescope. These molecules were found to coexist in a specific interstellar cloud, suggesting their simultaneous formation through common chemical pathways. Two distinct chemical processes, namely the combination of ethynyl radicals with acetylene and the addition of a hydrogen atom to vinyl cyanide, are thought to be responsible for the formation of the ethynyl and cyano variants of hydrocarbon rings, respectively. While the former mechanism is limited by the availability of dimers, the latter is facilitated by the presence of HCN and HNC. Through the analysis of spectral data from multiple sources, we've calculated the relative abundances of six types of hydrocarbon rings, namely CH, CN, CC, CN, NC, CCCH, and CNCCH, in the TMC-1 cloud. Our results show that carbon-rich species are more abundant than their nitrogen counterparts, with a notable exception of the cyclopentadiene ring, which exhibits a higher abundance of its cyano counterpart.

In models where the dark matter forms through gravitational trapping, we find that the formation process can lead to a range of DM mass distributions. This result has significant implications for searches for DM using gravitational waves and for experiments that detect DM interactions, as the non-uniform mass distribution DM candidates will have distinct effects on these searches.

Using 36.1 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ of 13 TeV proton--proton collision data, the study investigates the $pp \rightarrow t\bar{t}Z$ process in electron--muon channels with the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. It sets an upper limit on four-lepton pair distributions for $t\bar{t}Z$ production and observes no significant deviations from standard model predictions.
